desc_declarative_claude:
The module models a simplified registration system that tracks a person's birth year and whether they have been issued a driver's license, illustrating the Y2K (Year 2000) problem caused by two-digit year storage.

Two constants parameterize the model: `BIRTH_YEAR`, the person's birth year stored as a two-digit integer (0–99), and `LICENSE_AGE`, the minimum age required to obtain a license (1–99). The two variables are `year`, representing the current year as a two-digit integer, and `hasLicense`, a Boolean indicating whether a license has been issued. Initially, `year` equals `BIRTH_YEAR` and no license has been issued. The `NewYear` action advances the year by incrementing it modulo 100, faithfully reproducing the two-digit overflow bug. The `IssueLicense` action grants a license whenever the computed age (`year - BIRTH_YEAR`) is at least `LICENSE_AGE`. Because the year wraps around modulo 100, `Age` can become negative or artificially small after the wraparound, allowing the system to issue a license prematurely or causing a previously valid license to appear invalid.

The module defines two invariants. `Inv` is a type-correctness invariant asserting that `year` stays within 0–99 and `hasLicense` is a Boolean. `Safety` expresses the intended property that a license holder must currently satisfy the minimum age requirement; this invariant is explicitly noted as being violated due to the year wraparound bug.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a reconfigurable Paxos-style consensus algorithm with acceptors casting votes across instances and ballots, and with reconfiguration commands that change the active configuration. The state consists of per-acceptor votes `avote` and a set `learned` of learned instance-command pairs; the spec defines when votes are cast, when an acceptor abstains, when a value is learned, and how configurations are derived from learned reconfiguration commands. The file proves safety properties only, not liveness: it states the standard temporal specification `Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<avote, learned>>`, proves type correctness and a safety invariant, and then develops a substantial TLAPS proof showing an inductive invariant for reconfiguration safety.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies a reconfigurable multi-instance Paxos consensus algorithm, where configurations (sets of quorums) can themselves be changed by choosing special reconfiguration commands. The system models a fixed set of acceptors (`Acc`) and two variables: `avote`, a three-dimensional function mapping each acceptor, instance number, and ballot number to either a vote record (carrying a configuration number and command), the special value `init` (uncast), or `none` (abstained); and `learned`, a set of pairs recording which commands have been learned in which instance numbers.

The initial state sets all votes to `init` and places the initial configuration command at instance −1 in `learned`. Three actions drive the system: `VoteFor` lets an acceptor cast a vote in a given instance and ballot, subject to consistency with other votes in that ballot, safety conditions (`SafeAt`), and configuration validity (`ConfigOKAt`); `Abstain` lets an acceptor mark a set of instance-ballot pairs as abstained; and `Learn` adds a command to `learned` when it has been chosen (via a quorum of matching votes) under a valid configuration. The next-state relation `Next` is the disjunction of all such steps, and the temporal specification `Spec` is the standard safety-only formula `Init /\ [][Next]_<<avote, learned>>` with no fairness conditions.

The module states and partially proves two theorems: that `TypeOK` is an invariant, and that the key safety property `SafetyInv`—asserting that at most one command is ever learned per instance—is an invariant. The proof proceeds through an inductive invariant `Inv` with five conjuncts, covering type correctness, ballot-level vote uniqueness, justification of learned entries, well-formedness of the configuration sequence (`CfgOK`), and a detailed `SafeAt`/`ConfigOKAt` witness property for every vote. Stability lemmas for votes, chosen values, and configuration predicates support the inductiveness argument.

desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies Dijkstra's distributed termination detection algorithm on a ring (EWD 840). The system consists of N nodes arranged in a ring, each of which can be active or inactive and colored white or black. A single token circulates around the ring, also carrying a color. The four variables are `active` (a Boolean map over nodes), `color` (a color map over nodes), `tpos` (the current token position), and `tcolor` (the token's color). Initially the token color is black; all other variables may take any type-correct values.

The next-state relation splits into two parts. The `System` actions implement the detection protocol: node 0 initiates a new probe when it holds the token and either it or the token is black, resetting the token to white and itself to white; any other node holding the token passes it to its predecessor, possibly staining the token black if the node itself is black, then whitening itself. These system actions are subject to weak fairness. The `Environment` actions model the underlying computation: an active node may send a message to any other node (activating it and potentially turning the sender black if the message travels against the token direction), or any active node may spontaneously deactivate. Together these actions define a temporal specification `Spec` asserting the initial condition, the always-enabled next-state relation as a safety constraint, and weak fairness of the token-passing actions. The module defines `TypeOK` as a type invariant but does not explicitly state liveness or correctness properties within this file.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models the Paxos consensus algorithm, focusing on its safety properties and omitting explicit leader and learner processes. The model uses a message-passing abstraction, where the set of all messages ever sent is tracked, rather than modeling messages in transit or message loss. The algorithm is parameterized by sets of values, acceptors, and quorums, and models the core Paxos phases (1a, 1b, 2a, 2b) as actions, with state variables representing the highest ballot seen, the highest ballot voted for, and the value voted for by each acceptor. The specification includes a type invariant, an initial state, and a refinement mapping to a Voting module, as well as an inductive invariant for proof purposes. Liveness is only partially addressed, with the main focus on safety.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies the classic Paxos consensus algorithm as a message-passing system, without explicit leader or learner processes. It is instantiated with concrete constants: values `{1, 2}`, acceptors `{1, 2, 3}`, quorums `{{1,2},{2,3},{1,3}}`, and ballots `1..3`.

The state consists of four variables: `maxBal` (the highest ballot number each acceptor has promised to respect), `maxVBal` and `maxVal` (the ballot and value of each acceptor's highest-numbered vote), and `msgs` (the monotonically growing set of all messages ever sent). Four message types are modeled: phase-1a (ballot proposals), phase-1b (acceptor promises with their current vote state), phase-2a (leader value proposals), and phase-2b (acceptor votes).

The next-state relation comprises four actions. `Phase1a(b)` broadcasts a phase-1a message opening ballot `b`. `Phase1b(a)` allows acceptor `a` to respond to a phase-1a message whose ballot exceeds `maxBal[a]`, updating `maxBal[a]` and sending its prior vote information. `Phase2a(b,v)` allows a leader to propose value `v` in ballot `b` provided no phase-2a message for `b` exists yet and a quorum of phase-1b responses demonstrates that `v` is safe (either no prior votes exist in the quorum or the highest prior vote was for `v`). `Phase2b(a)` lets acceptor `a` vote for a proposed value if the proposal's ballot is at least `maxBal[a]`. The temporal specification is `Init ∧ [][Next]_vars` with no fairness conditions, targeting safety verification. The module defines an inductive invariant `Inv` asserting type correctness, consistency of per-acceptor vote records, and that every phase-2a message proposes a value shown safe by some quorum, supporting a refinement mapping to an abstract voting specification.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a simple producer-consumer style system with two state variables: a set S representing stored produced items and a Boolean flag empty indicating whether the storage is empty. The initial state sets S to the empty set and empty to TRUE. The Produce action makes the system non-empty and adds one chosen subset of a fixed finite alphabet to S, while the Consume action is enabled only when the system is not empty and replaces S with an arbitrary subset of its current contents, updating empty to reflect whether the resulting set is empty; the file defines Init, Produce, Consume, and Next but does not include a full temporal specification or fairness conditions.
desc_declarative_claude: The module specifies a simple producer-consumer system operating over a shared set `S` and a Boolean flag `empty`. Initially, `S` is the empty set and `empty` is `TRUE`. The `Produce` action sets `empty` to `FALSE` and non-deterministically adds some subset of the alphabet `{"A", "B", "Z", "1", "8"}` to `S`, growing the shared collection. The `Consume` action is enabled only when `empty` is `FALSE`; it non-deterministically replaces `S` with any subset of its current contents, and updates `empty` to reflect whether the resulting set is empty. The next-state relation is the disjunction of these two actions. The module defines no explicit invariants, liveness properties, or fairness conditions, and includes no temporal specification formula beyond the implicit use of `Init` and `Next`. It is a minimal behavioral model illustrating how a producer adds items to a shared set and a consumer removes items, with the `empty` flag tracking whether the set has been fully consumed.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module models an asynchronous Byzantine agreement protocol based on the Bracha-Toueg protocol, using counters for sent and received ECHO and READY messages together with per-process program counters. The fault model is Byzantine with up to F faulty processes, under the assumption N > 3 * T, T >= F, and F >= 0, and faults are introduced explicitly by a BecomeByzantine action. The specification defines initial states, step actions, a next-state relation, weak fairness for message receipt and protocol progress actions, and temporal properties for type correctness, unforgeability-style safety, eventual acceptance when all start with value 1, and eventual agreement after some process accepts.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies the asynchronous Byzantine consensus protocol of Bracha and Toueg (1985), Figure 3, using a counting abstraction over N processes, at most F of which may be Byzantine (with the resilience condition N > 3T ≥ 3F ≥ 0).

Each process has a program counter drawn from {"V0", "V1", "EC", "RD", "AC", "BYZ"}, representing its initial proposal (0 or 1), the ECHO and READY phases, the accepted state, and the Byzantine state. Rather than modeling individual messages, the spec tracks aggregate counts: the total number of ECHO and READY messages sent (nSntE, nSntR), each process's received counts (nRcvdE, nRcvdR), and the current number of Byzantine processes (nByz). A process can become Byzantine (up to F total), receive messages one at a time (bounded by sent plus Byzantine counts), send an ECHO message when its proposal or received-message thresholds are met, send a READY message after echoing and receiving sufficient messages, or decide (move to "AC") after receiving at least 2T+1 READY messages. Three initialization predicates cover mixed proposals, all-zero proposals, and all-one proposals.

The temporal specification Spec (and Spec0 for the all-zero case) pairs the Init condition and the Next-state relation with weak fairness over all non-Byzantine process actions. Three LTL properties are stated: Unforg\_Ltl (if all processes propose 0, no process ever decides), Corr\_Ltl (if all propose 1, some process eventually decides), and Agreement\_Ltl (if any process decides, eventually all non-Byzantine processes decide).

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a parameterized reliable broadcast algorithm by message diffusion under crash failures. Processes may start either with an initial value indicating they have received the broadcast or without it, may receive ECHO messages, may accept and rebroadcast ECHO, and up to F correct processes may crash. The specification includes initializations with and without an initial broadcast, a safety-oriented type invariant, temporal specifications with weak fairness for receive-and-accept behavior, and liveness/safety properties such as no forgery, correctness of propagation, relay, and reliable channel delivery.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies a parameterized model of reliable broadcast by message diffusion with crash failures, based on the algorithm of Chandra and Toueg (1996). It models N processes (indexed 1..N), up to F of which may crash, with a fault-tolerance threshold T. The only message type is "ECHO".

The state is tracked via `pc` (each process's program counter, taking values V0, V1, AC, or CR), `rcvd` (messages received per process), `sent` (the global set of sent messages), `nCrashed` (count of crashed processes), and `Corr` (the current set of correct processes). Initially, no messages are sent or received, no process has crashed, and each process is nondeterministically in V0 (no INIT received) or V1 (INIT received), except in `InitNoBcast` where all start at V0.

In each step, a correct process first nondeterministically receives any superset of its current received messages that is a subset of `sent`, then either: transitions from V1 to AC and broadcasts ECHO (`UponV1`); transitions from V0 or V1 to AC and broadcasts ECHO upon receiving at least one message (`UponAccept`); crashes if the crash budget allows (`UponCrash`); or does nothing. The temporal specification `Spec` adds weak fairness over the non-crash actions to support liveness reasoning. A `SpecNoBcast` variant uses the no-broadcast initial condition.

The module defines a state-type invariant `sTypeOK`, and four properties: `Unforg`/`UnforgLtl` (if no process started with INIT, no correct process ever accepts), `CorrLtl` (if all correct processes hold V1, some eventually accepts), `RelayLtl` (once any correct process accepts, all correct processes eventually accept), and `ReliableChan` (any sent ECHO is eventually permanently received by all correct processes).

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a very small state-transition system over two variables, x and y. It defines a single action Next that constrains the next-state values of x and y through a conjunction of equalities and a nested disjunction, effectively specifying a cyclic dependency between the primed values x' and y'. The file does not declare an initial predicate, temporal specification, fairness condition, proof, or fault model; it only gives the transition relation.
desc_declarative_claude: The module defines a trivially unsatisfiable next-state relation over two variables, `x` and `y`. The `Next` action requires simultaneously that either `x'` equals 1, or both `y'` equals 1 and `x'` equals 2, while also demanding the contradictory circular equalities `x' = y'` and `y' = x'` alongside the disjunctive assignments. Because the first disjunct sets `x'` to 1 while the second sets `x'` to 2 but both branches must satisfy `x' = y'`, and there is no initial-state predicate or temporal formula defined, the module is essentially an incomplete fragment. It declares no `Init`, no `Spec`, and no invariants or properties — only the `Next` relation and the two variables. This appears to be a minimal or test module, likely used to explore how TLA+ handles unsatisfiable or contradictory conjunctions in a next-state relation rather than to model any real system or algorithm.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies the NBAC (non-blocking atomic commitment) algorithm with crash failures and a per-process failure detector. Processes vote YES or NO, send their votes as messages, receive nondeterministically delivered messages, may crash, and then decide ABORT or COMMIT depending on received votes and the detector state. The specification defines an initial condition, a next-state relation over program counters, received and sent messages, and detector outputs, and checks typing and a validity property; it also includes a weak fairness condition in Spec to ensure fair progress of certain enabled receive/send/decision behavior.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies the Non-Blocking Atomic Commitment (NBAC) protocol with process crashes, following the algorithm described by Raynal (1997). It models a distributed system of N processes that must collectively decide to either commit or abort a transaction.

The state is captured by four variables: `pc` (each process's program counter, ranging over YES, NO, SENT, ABORT, COMMIT, and CRASH), `sent` (the global set of messages sent as process-message pairs), `rcvd` (messages received by each process), and `fd` (a per-process boolean failure detector flag indicating whether any crash has been suspected). Processes begin in either the YES or NO state (nondeterministically in `Init`, or all YES in `InitAllYes`), with no messages sent or received.

Each step for a process nondeterministically receives a subset of sent messages, updates its failure detector reading, and then takes one of several actions: send a YES or NO vote (transitioning to SENT), crash at any time, decide ABORT if a NO message is received or a crash is suspected, decide COMMIT only if all N processes have sent YES and no crash is suspected, or do nothing to prevent deadlock. The temporal specification `Spec` combines `Init`, the always-enabled `Next` relation, and a weak fairness condition ensuring that non-crash steps (voting and deciding) eventually execute if continuously enabled.

The invariant `TypeOK` enforces type correctness, and `Validity` asserts that a process can commit only if all processes initially voted YES. A liveness property (`NonTriv`) is present but commented out.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a parameterized asynchronous non-blocking atomic commitment algorithm with failure detectors, following the Guerraoui 2001 paper cited in the comments. The model tracks how processes initially vote YES or NO, may crash and become Byzantine-marked via the "BYZ" status, send messages, receive YES/NO messages, abort, or commit, while a failure detector variable records suspicion information. The specification defines three initializations (arbitrary votes, all YES, all NO), a next-state relation with weak fairness for message-processing and decision actions, and temporal properties for agreement, abort validity, commit validity, and termination.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies a parameterized, threshold-based abstraction of Guerraoui's asynchronous Non-Blocking Atomic Commitment (NBAC) algorithm with failure detectors, as described in IPL 2001. The system models N processes, each holding a program counter (`pc`) initialized to either "YES" or "NO" (its vote). Rather than tracking individual messages, the spec uses integer counters: `nSntYes` and `nSntNo` count votes broadcast by correct processes, while `nSntYesF` and `nSntNoF` bound the number of messages faulty processes may have sent before crashing. Each process's received-message counts (`nRcvdYes`, `nRcvdNo`) are incremented up to those totals. The boolean array `someFail` models a perfect failure detector: a process is suspected only if it crashes, and every crashed process is eventually suspected.

The key actions are: `Crash`, which moves a process to the "BYZ" state and may increment the faulty-message bounds; `SendYes`/`SendNo`, which broadcast a vote if the process is unsuspected; `AbortNoYes`, which aborts an unsent process that is suspected; `AbortSent`, which aborts after receiving at least one NO; `Commit`, which commits once a process has received N YES votes and no NO votes; and `Receive`, which increments message counters. Three specifications (`Spec`, `SpecYes`, `SpecNo`) combine respective initialization predicates with the always-`Next` safety constraint and weak fairness over all progress actions. The module checks a `TypeOK` invariant, an agreement safety property (`AgrrLtl`) preventing simultaneous COMMIT and ABORT decisions, abort and commit validity properties, and a conditional termination liveness property.

desc_declarative_gpt: This TLA+ specification models Dijkstra's distributed termination detection algorithm for a ring of N nodes, as described in EWD 840. The system consists of nodes that can be active or passive, each with a color (white or black), and a circulating token with a position and color. The algorithm detects global termination by passing a token around the ring and using color changes to track activity. The specification defines the possible actions: initiating a probe, passing the token, sending messages (which may activate other nodes and change colors), and deactivating nodes. The temporal property ensures that the system starts in a type-correct initial state with a black token, and that all steps follow the defined next-state relation, with weak fairness for the system actions. The model assumes N is a positive natural number and does not explicitly model faults.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies Dijkstra's distributed termination detection algorithm for a ring of N nodes, known as EWD 840. The system models a ring of nodes (indexed 0 to N−1) where nodes can be active or inactive and exchange messages, alongside a token-passing mechanism that detects when all computation has ceased.

The four variables are: `active`, a mapping from nodes to booleans indicating whether each node is currently computing; `color`, a mapping from nodes to either "white" or "black" encoding whether a node has sent a message in the "wrong" direction since last whitened; `tpos`, the current position of the token; and `tcolor`, the color of the token. Initially, the token is black and all other variables may take any type-correct values.

The next-state relation is split into System and Environment actions. System actions implement the detection algorithm: node 0 initiates a new probe (resetting the token to white) when it holds a black token or is itself black, and any other node holding the token passes it leftward, potentially blackening it and whitening itself. Environment actions model the underlying computation: an active node may send a message to any other node (blackening itself if it sends to a higher-numbered node, i.e., against the token direction), or any active node may spontaneously deactivate. The temporal specification `Spec` requires weak fairness on System actions, ensuring the token-passing protocol continues making progress. The invariant `TypeOK` asserts well-typedness of all variables.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a message-passing version of the Paxos consensus algorithm without explicit leaders or learners. It models acceptors, ballots, quorums, and the accumulation of all sent messages in a single set variable, focusing primarily on safety rather than realistic message transport behavior such as loss, duplication, or delivery. The specification defines the phase 1a, phase 1b, phase 2a, and phase 2b actions, gives a standard temporal specification `Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars`, and includes copied helper predicates from a Voting-style abstraction plus an inductive invariant candidate relating acceptor vote state to the recorded vote messages.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies the classic Paxos consensus algorithm as a message-passing system, without explicit leader or learner processes. It is parameterized with concrete constants: four acceptors ("a1"–"a4"), two values ({0, 1}), ballots ranging over 1..10, and four three-element quorums drawn from the acceptors, satisfying the quorum intersection assumption.

The state consists of four variables: `maxBal` (the highest ballot number each acceptor has promised to respect), `maxVBal` and `maxVal` (the ballot number and value of each acceptor's most recent vote), and `msgs` (the ever-growing set of all messages ever sent, modeling a reliable message history). The four message types cover the two phases of Paxos: 1a (ballot-open), 1b (promise with prior vote), 2a (propose), and 2b (vote). The four actions are `Phase1a` (broadcast a phase-1a message for ballot b), `Phase1b` (an acceptor responds with its current state if the ballot exceeds its promise), `Phase2a` (propose a value for ballot b once a quorum of 1b messages establishes safety), and `Phase2b` (an acceptor votes for the proposed value and updates its local state). The next-state relation `Next` is the disjunction of all these actions, and the temporal specification is `Init ∧ [][Next]_vars` without fairness.

The module also defines a partial inductive invariant `Inv` asserting that each acceptor's recorded vote is consistent with the actual votes cast, and includes auxiliary definitions (`VotedFor`, `ShowsSafeAt`) copied from a companion `Voting` module to support a refinement mapping, though the refinement theorem itself is commented out.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies the Paxos consensus algorithm in an abstract message-passing style without explicit leaders or learners. It models acceptors tracking their highest promised ballot and highest voted ballot/value, and models communication via a monotonically growing set of sent messages rather than explicit in-transit delivery, emphasizing safety over network behavior. The spec defines the standard Paxos phase 1 and phase 2 actions, a next-state relation and safety-oriented invariant, and includes a refinement-oriented reconstruction of voting information together with copied predicates from a Voting specification to express safe value selection.
desc_declarative_claude:
The Paxos module specifies the classic Paxos consensus algorithm in a message-passing style, without explicit leader or learner processes. It is instantiated with concrete constants: three acceptors (`{1, 2, 3}`), three majority quorums, two possible values (`{1, 2}`), and ballots drawn from `1..3`.

The four variables are `maxBal`, `maxVBal`, and `maxVal` (per-acceptor state tracking the highest promised ballot, highest voted ballot, and corresponding value) and `msgs` (the monotonically growing set of all messages ever sent). Messages are of four types: 1a (ballot initiation), 1b (promise from acceptor), 2a (value proposal), and 2b (vote by acceptor).

The five key actions implement the two-phase protocol. `Phase1a(b)` broadcasts a phase-1a message for ballot `b`. `Phase1b(a)` has acceptor `a` respond to a 1a message with a higher ballot by promising and reporting its last vote. `Phase2a(b, v)` allows a leader to propose value `v` in ballot `b`, provided no 2a for that ballot exists yet and a quorum of 1b messages demonstrates that `v` is safe (via the quorum-based safe-value condition). `Phase2b(a)` has an acceptor vote for the proposed value if the ballot is at least its current `maxBal`. The overall specification is `Init /\ [][Next]_vars` with no fairness constraints, so only safety is directly enforced.

The module defines a refinement mapping to a `Voting` module through the derived `votes` function, along with auxiliary predicates `VotedFor`, `DidNotVoteAt`, and `ShowsSafeAt`. The inductive invariant `Inv` asserts type correctness, consistency between per-acceptor state and the votes record, and that 1b and 2a messages faithfully reflect protocol history, including uniqueness of proposed values per ballot.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a simple spanning-tree construction protocol over a fixed directed neighbor relation on a set of processes. Initially every process has no parent, no process has reported, and no sent-message flag is set; processes can send discovery messages along edges, adopt a parent when they receive a message while parentless and not the root, and later mark themselves as reported. The spec defines a temporal behavior with weak fairness on the main next-state action, and it asserts typing, an eventual spanning-tree property, an invariant-like one-parent stability property, and a predicate constraining when parentless non-root processes may have sent messages.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies an Asynchronous Spanning Tree (AST) construction algorithm over a fixed directed graph of processes. The graph is concretely defined with N = 4 processes (1..4), a distinguished root process (process 1), and a neighbor relation where process p is a neighbor of q exactly when p < q, forming a directed acyclic ordering. The three variables are `parent`, a mapping from each process to its parent (or NULL if none assigned yet); `reported`, a Boolean flag per process indicating whether it has acknowledged having a parent; and `sntMsg`, a Boolean matrix recording which directed messages have been sent between processes.

In the initial state all parents are NULL, no process has reported, and no messages have been sent. The key actions are: `Send`, which allows a process that is either the root or already has a parent to send a message to a neighbor it has not yet messaged; `Update`, which assigns a parent to a non-root process upon receiving a message from a neighbor when it has no parent yet; and `Parent`, which allows a process with a non-NULL parent to set its reported flag. The `Next` relation gives priority to `Update` when applicable, otherwise allowing `Send`, `Parent`, or stuttering. The specification includes weak fairness over the entire next-state relation. Checked properties include a `TypeOK` type invariant, the liveness property `SpanningTree` asserting that eventually every non-root process acquires a valid parent, the safety property `OneParent` asserting that parent assignments are permanent once made, and `SntMsg` asserting that only processes with a parent (or the root) may send messages.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a small Paxos-style consensus protocol without explicit leaders or learners, using message passing and a global set of sent messages. It models phase 1a, phase 1b, phase 2a, and phase 2b messages, tracks acceptor promise and vote state, and defines a refinement-oriented view of votes from sent phase 2b messages. The specification focuses primarily on safety rather than realistic message transport, explicitly noting that message loss and duplication are not modeled because safety depends only on which messages may be received; it also includes an inductive invariant and helper definitions copied from a Voting specification to express safe value selection.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies a simplified version of the Paxos consensus algorithm without explicit leader or learner processes, operating over a fixed set of three acceptors, two values, and three ballot numbers. The four variables are `maxBal` (the highest ballot number each acceptor has promised to respect), `maxVBal` and `maxVal` (the ballot number and value of the highest-numbered vote each acceptor has cast), and `msgs` (the ever-growing set of all messages sent, serving as a reliable broadcast medium).

The four actions correspond to the standard Paxos phases. `Phase1a(b)` broadcasts a prepare message for ballot `b`. `Phase1b(a)` lets acceptor `a` respond to a prepare message for any ballot exceeding its current `maxBal`, updating that bound and reporting its highest prior vote. `Phase2a(b, v)` fires when no phase-2a message for ballot `b` exists yet and a quorum of phase-1b responses establishes that value `v` is safe at `b` — either because no quorum member has voted before, or because `v` matches the value voted in the highest prior ballot among quorum members. `Phase2b(a)` lets acceptor `a` cast a vote for the value in any phase-2a message whose ballot meets or exceeds `a`'s current `maxBal`. Notably, the `Next` relation includes only `Phase2a`, making `Spec` a heavily restricted behavior used for refinement checking rather than full execution. The module defines a `votes` function mapping acceptors to their phase-2b votes, copies the `ShowsSafeAt` predicate from the companion `Voting` module, and states an inductive invariant `Inv` capturing type correctness, vote-record consistency, and the safety of every phase-2a message sent.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a very small transition system over two variables, a and b. desc_declarative_claude: This is a small TLA+ module that explores logical negation within a next-state relation. It declares two variables, `a` and `b`, with `Init` only constraining `a` to equal 0 (leaving `b` unconstrained). The `Next` action is the conjunction of two conditions: the negation of `(a' = 1 ∧ b' = 2)` and the assertion that `(a' = 2 ∧ b' = 2)`. Because the second conjunct forces `a' = 2` and `b' = 2`, the negated first conjunct is automatically satisfied (since `a' = 2 ≠ 1`), making the negation redundant in practice. The temporal specification `Spec` is a standard safety formula asserting that every step either satisfies `Next` or leaves `a` unchanged (a stuttering step). No liveness or fairness conditions are included, and no invariants or properties are declared for model checking. This module appears to be a minimal demonstration or test of how TLA+ handles negation of conjunctions within a next-state predicate rather than a model of any real system or algorithm.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a very small two-variable state machine over variables a and b. The temporal property Spec asserts the stuttering-closed next-state specification [][Next]_<< a,b >>.
desc_declarative_claude:
This is a small TLA+ module that models a two-variable system and tests how simultaneous assignments interact when primed variables reference each other within set-membership expressions.

The module declares two variables, `a` and `b`, both initialized to zero. The `Next` action is a conjunction of two parts. The right conjunct unconditionally constrains `a'` to the singleton set `{1}`, so `a` always becomes 1 on any step. The left conjunct offers a disjunctive choice: either both `a'` is in `{b'}` and `b'` is in `{a'}` simultaneously (a mutually referential constraint that, combined with the right conjunct fixing `a'` to 1, forces `b'` to 1 as well), or `b'` is in `{2}` (making `b` become 2). The temporal specification `Spec` is a stuttering-closed safety property expressed as `[][Next]_<<a,b>>`, permitting either a `Next` step or a stuttering step that leaves both variables unchanged. desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a very small two-variable state machine over variables a and b. desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a very small state machine over two variables, a and b. The initial state sets both variables to 0. desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a very small state machine with two state variables, a and b. desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a simple system with two variables, a and b, both initialized to 0.
