The file does not define a transition system or temporal behavior of its own; instead, it encodes assertion-style validation of imported graph operators such as SimplePath, ConnectedComponents, AreConnectedIn, and IsStronglyConnected.

This module is a test specification for vector clock causality utilities imported from the VectorClocks module. It asserts a series of assumptions over small example traces and over a log loaded from an NDJSON file, checking whether IsCausalOrder classifies traces as causal or non-causal under various vector-clock and node projections. The specification uses helper operators to extract vector clocks and node identifiers from deserialized log entries, and it documents a JSON deserialization design issue where numeric object keys become record fields with string domains, requiring ToString conversion.

This module specifies the Fast Paxos consensus algorithm, modeling coordinators, acceptors, proposals, learning, retransmission, message loss, leader changes, and failure/repair of agents. The fault model includes arbitrary message loss except for the most recent message of a good agent, and arbitrary changes to the set of good agents and to coordinator leadership; progress is then stated under fairness assumptions and an eventual stable-goodness condition LA(c, Q). The specification defines both safety and progress aspects: safety through invariants such as type correctness, nontriviality, and consistency, and liveness through fairness constraints on good coordinators, good acceptors, and learning actions, together with a theorem that eventual stability implies eventual learning.

This specification models Lamport's Bakery algorithm for mutual exclusion among N processes. The algorithm is specified using a PlusCal algorithm block, which is then translated into TLA+ actions and temporal properties. The model includes the lexicographic ordering relation for ticket numbers, and defines the state variables, process actions, and the main temporal specification. The specification verifies mutual exclusion, type correctness, and includes a detailed inductive invariant (Inv) with a full TLAPS proof of mutual exclusion. The model assumes a crash-free, asynchronous system with no faults, and is designed for both model checking and deductive verification.

This module specifies and proves correctness of a PlusCal encoding of the Boulangerie algorithm, a variant of Lamport's bakery-style mutual exclusion algorithm due to Moses and Patkin. It models the translated per-process control-location actions, proves type correctness and mutual exclusion with TLAPS, and states liveness properties for deadlock freedom and starvation freedom under weak fairness.

This specification models the Car Talk puzzle from the 22 October 2011 program, in which a farmer must break a 40-pound stone into 4 pieces so that any integer weight from 1 to 40 pounds can be measured using a balance scale and those pieces. The spec generalizes the problem to breaking an N-pound stone into P pieces, with N and P as constants. It defines the set of all possible breaks (ways to partition the stone), checks which breaks allow all weights to be measured (solutions), and provides a way to enumerate all such solutions. The design uses recursive summation, set and function constructs, and quantification to capture the combinatorial structure of the problem. The spec is intended for use with TLC, which can compute the set of all solutions for given N and P.

This specification models the Car Talk puzzle from the 22 October 2011 program, in which a farmer must break a 40-pound stone into 4 pieces so that any integer weight from 1 to 40 pounds can be measured using a balance scale and those pieces. The spec generalizes the problem to breaking an N-pound stone into P pieces, with N and P as constants. It defines a 'break' as a function from 1..P to 1..N (the weights of the pieces), constrained to be non-decreasing and sum to N. The main property verified is that for every weight w in 1..N, there exist two disjoint subsets of the pieces such that w plus the sum of one subset equals the sum of the other, i.e., the weight can be balanced. The specification computes all such solutions and provides an expanded form showing, for each solution and each weight, how to arrange the pieces on the scale. The design avoids ambiguity from identical weights by using functions rather than sets for breaks, and includes comments explaining all nonstandard TLA+ notation.

This specification models the Car Talk puzzle from the 22 October 2011 program, in which a farmer must break a 40-pound stone into 4 pieces so that any integer weight from 1 to 40 pounds can be measured using a balance scale and those pieces. The spec generalizes the problem to breaking an N-pound stone into P pieces, with N and P as constants. It defines a 'break' as a function from 1..P to 1..N (the weights of the pieces), constrained so the pieces are in non-decreasing order and sum to N. The main property verified is that for every weight w in 1..N, there exist two disjoint subsets of pieces that can be placed on opposite sides of the scale to balance w. The specification computes all such solutions and provides an operator to expand and display them, illustrating how each weight can be measured. The design uses recursive operators, set comprehensions, and Hilbert's CHOOSE to express the solution space.

This module specifies the Car Talk balance-scale puzzle about breaking an N-pound stone into P integer-weight pieces so that any integral weight from 1 through N can be weighed using a balance. It models candidate breaks as nondecreasing functions from 1..P to 1..N, defines when a target weight is representable by placing some pieces on each side of the scale, and characterizes solutions as breaks that represent every weight in 1..N. The spec is not a transition system with variables or temporal behavior; instead it is a mathematical specification intended for TLC evaluation of the set of all solutions, with an auxiliary operator that expands each solution into explicit weighing instructions.

This specification models checkpoint coordination in a replicated Paxos/RSL-style cluster with node failures, network failures, leader election, replicated requests, and lease-based authorization for checkpointing. It separates environment state, Paxos-related state, and checkpoint-specific state, and uses replicated log entries plus checkpoint leases to ensure that at most one eligible node checkpoints at a time while preserving log consistency. The spec verifies a type invariant, a safety invariant about lease ownership and non-conflicting logs, and temporal expectations that checkpoint opportunities and completions eventually occur under stated fairness assumptions.

This module provides a TLAPS proof that the CoffeeCan specification maintains the TypeInvariant property throughout execution. The proof strengthens the invariant by adding a bound on the total number of beans (BeanCount) to ensure that the bean count never exceeds MaxBeanCount, which is necessary because certain actions could otherwise violate this bound. The proof is structured hierarchically and covers all possible actions, showing that each action preserves the invariant and that the system is type-correct under the specified dynamics.

This specification models the classic Coffee Can problem, where a can contains black and white beans and repeatedly removes two beans according to their colors, possibly adding back a black bean. The model represents the can as a record with black and white counts bounded by a constant maximum, and it studies the effect of the three possible bean-selection cases plus a termination stuttering action when only one bean remains. The spec checks a type invariant, monotonic decrease in total bean count, eventual termination under weak fairness, preservation of the parity of the white-bean count, and a hypothesis that the final bean is black iff the initial number of white beans is even.

This module is an Apalache-compatible wrapper around another specification, DieHardest, for model checking only the interleaved-composition part of the system described as Section 4. The comments explain that the original DieHardest specification uses TLC-specific operators in Sections 1-3, so this wrapper avoids those and instead provides constant initialization and capacity functions in a form acceptable to Apalache. The module declares constants for capacities and goal, variables for two capacity maps and two scalar states, instantiates the DieHardest module, and defines helper operators that set up a specific model-checking scenario with two candidate capacity configurations and a fixed goal value.

This module provides a TLAPS proof that the DieHard water jug puzzle specification maintains the TypeOK invariant throughout all behaviors. The proof shows that the initial state satisfies TypeOK and that every step of the Next action preserves TypeOK, using case analysis on each possible action (FillSmallJug, FillBigJug, EmptySmallJug, EmptyBigJug, SmallToBig, BigToSmall, and stuttering steps). The proof leverages the Min operator and its properties, as well as arithmetic reasoning about the jug capacities. The NotSolved invariant is intentionally not proved, as it is meant to be violated to find a solution to the puzzle.

This specification models the generalized Die Hard water-jug problem with an arbitrary set of jugs, a capacity function assigning each jug a positive integer capacity, and a target amount of water called Goal. The state consists of a single variable contents mapping each jug to its current water amount, and the system evolves by filling a jug, emptying a jug, or pouring from one jug into another by the maximum amount possible. The spec assumes only well-formed capacities and a natural-number goal, uses a standard stuttering-inclusive temporal specification Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_contents, and defines NotSolved as the safety property that no jug currently contains the goal amount; the comments explain that TLC can search for a counterexample to this invariant to produce a solution trace.

This module models a self-composition of two jug-filling systems in order to analyze a 2-hyperproperty about which of two Die Hard configurations reaches a target amount of water in fewer steps. It compares several composition styles: lock-step parallel composition, per-behavior freezing, TLC-specific global BFS-level freezing, and finally an interleaved composition that gives a clean TLA+ solution. The specification assumes both configurations are solvable, assumes TLC is running in single-worker BFS mode so counterexamples are shortest, and uses the final interleaved specification to obtain shortest step counts s1 and s2 for the two independent instances.

This module is a thin Apalache-oriented wrapper around a separate helper module named RingBuffer. It introduces typed constants and a single variable ringbuffer, then instantiates RingBuffer so that the helper module can be typechecked in isolation. The comments explain that the underlying helper module defines Init and parameterized actions such as Write, EndWrite, BeginRead, and EndRead, but this wrapper itself does not define Next, temporal behavior, or fault handling, and leaves preservation of NoDataRaces to concrete protocol modules such as Disruptor_SPMC.

This module specifies a ring buffer abstraction with a fixed number of slots indexed modulo the buffer size. Each slot stores either a value from Values or the distinguished NULL value, and the module additionally tracks the sets of readers and writers currently accessing each slot in order to model multi-step reads and writes. The specification provides initialization, index computation, begin/end read and write actions, and invariants such as type correctness and absence of data races; comments explicitly state that client specifications using this module should include NoDataRaces as an invariant.

This module provides Apalache-specific type annotations and concrete helper values for a distributed replicated log specification. It models a system with a set of servers, a set of values, an integer lag constant, and a single state variable cLogs mapping each server to a sequence of values representing its current log. The module also instantiates another module named DistributedReplicatedLog, but this file itself only defines the typed variable tuple vars and two concrete set-valued helper operators for servers and values; it contains no actions, temporal specification, fairness, or proof content.

This specification models a state-based CRDT counter replicated across a finite set of nodes. Each node stores a vector-like map of counts for every node, local increments update only the originating node's own component, and gossip merges copy pointwise maxima from one node's view into another node's view. The spec assumes Node is finite, defines safety and monotonicity properties over the replicated counter state, and introduces a fairness/liveness package asserting weak fairness for gossip and that eventually only gossip steps occur; it also states a convergence property that all node views are repeatedly eventually equal.

This module specifies an abstract distributed replicated log system in which each server maintains a local committed log and can either copy entries from a longer log or extend its own log. The model assumes a strong shared-state style fault-free view in which a server can directly inspect the logs of all other servers, rather than communicating through messages; comments note that this is unrealistic for real distributed systems and contrast it with protocols such as Raft. The specification enforces a machine-closed fairness condition requiring weak fairness for both copying and extending at every server, proves an invariant bounding the lag between server logs, proves that every server keeps extending forever, and also defines a stronger synchronization property that is intentionally not guaranteed.

This module defines a generic operator MapThenFoldSet that, given a binary operator 'op', a base value, a mapping function 'f', a choice function 'choose', and a set S, applies 'f' to each element of S and then folds the results using 'op', starting from 'base'. The folding order is determined by the 'choose' function, which selects an element from a set; if 'choose' is not deterministic, the result may depend on the order unless 'op' is associative and commutative. The module comments explain the intended use and provide an example, and reference simpler versions of fold for sets, functions, and sequences in other modules. No temporal properties or state variables are present; this is a pure functional operator definition.

This module defines a collection of operators for reasoning about functions in TLA+, including restriction, range, pointwise operations, inverses, and properties such as injectivity, surjectivity, and bijectivity. It provides operators to restrict a function to a subset of its domain or to values satisfying a predicate, to check if one function is a restriction of another, and to compute the range of a function. The module also defines operators for constructing sets of injections, surjections, and bijections between sets, and for checking their existence. Additionally, it includes fold operations over functions, leveraging a local instance of the Folds module. The specification is utility-focused and does not model a distributed algorithm or system, nor does it specify temporal properties or fault models.

This specification models a replicated log in which nodes append transactions to a shared log and track, per node, how many log entries have been executed. The state consists of the sequence-valued log and a function executed mapping each node to a natural number, with actions for writing a new transaction and for executing pending transactions. The spec states type correctness and safety, and studies convergence under different fairness assumptions, including sufficient fairness conditions that imply all nodes eventually catch up to the log length and several fairness variants that are identified as insufficient or effectively false.

This module provides Apalache-specific type annotations for a key-value store specification by declaring typed constants and variables and then instantiating the underlying KeyValueStore module. It does not define the algorithm itself in this file; instead, it supplies concrete constant sets and state variable declarations intended to match the imported specification's expected interface. The file contains no actions, temporal specification, fairness, assumptions, or proof content.

This module specifies client-centric isolation levels for transactional databases, following definitions from Crooks et al. It models database states as total functions from keys to values, operations as read/write records, transactions as sequences of operations, and executions as sequences pairing each transaction with its parent state. The spec defines helper predicates for read states, completeness, write sets, conflicts, transaction effects, and all possible executions, and then formalizes commit tests for Serializability, Snapshot Isolation, Strict Serializability, Read Committed, and Read Uncommitted, along with simple type predicates and a debug helper.

This module specifies a simple key-value store that supports transactions with snapshot isolation. Each transaction takes a snapshot of the store, chooses nonempty read and write key sets, reads from its snapshot, applies its writes locally, and then commits only if its write set does not conflict with keys missed due to concurrent committed transactions. The specification includes a PlusCal algorithm translated to TLA+, a temporal specification with weak fairness for each transaction process, a termination property, type correctness conditions, and client-centric isolation checks for snapshot isolation and serializability through an instantiated module.

This module provides a TLAPS proof for the temporal property Spec => [](TypeInvariant /\ TxLifecycle) of a key-value store system, as specified in KeyValueStore.tla. The proof demonstrates that the system maintains both type invariants and correct transaction lifecycles throughout its execution. The proof is structured hierarchically, showing that the invariants hold initially and are preserved by all possible transitions, including transaction operations and stuttering steps. The design leverages previously defined operators and actions from the KeyValueStore module, and uses TLAPS proof commands and structure to establish the result.

This specification models a simple key-value store with snapshot-isolated transactions. Each open transaction has its own snapshot of the store, a set of keys it has written, and a set of writes it has missed from other transactions; commits succeed only when there is no write-write conflict between the transaction's written keys and its missed keys. The spec defines transaction opening, add, update, remove, rollback, and close/commit steps, and proves that under the behavior specification the type invariant and transaction lifecycle cleanup properties always hold.

This module is a minimal wrapper around external modules. It extends KeyValueStore and TLC, and defines one top-level operator, TxIdSymmetric, as Permutations(TxId). The module itself contains no variables, actions, temporal formulas, assumptions, proofs, or PlusCal constructs.

This module defines general-purpose utility operators for TLA+ specifications rather than a complete transition-system model with variables and a behavioral Spec. It provides helpers for set intersection testing, maximum and minimum selection from a set, reduction over sets and sequences, sequence indexing and manipulation, conversion from sequences to sets, an intersection operator over a set of sets, permutation generation for finite sets, and a small testing helper that prints a diagnostic when two values differ. The module has no state variables, no actions, and no temporal correctness properties; it is purely a library of state-level and mathematical operators built using sets, sequences, choice, recursion through finite-domain function definitions, and TLC's Print operator.

This specification models a Knuth-Yao style stochastic state machine for generating one of the outcomes 1 through 6 by repeatedly tossing a fair coin and following a transition graph. The variables track the current dyadic probability mass p associated with the current node, the current control state, and the most recent coin flip. The specification initializes at state "s0" with probability One, evolves by halving p on each step and updating state through the Transition table, and asserts a standard temporal behavior consisting of initialization, next-state steps, and weak fairness of Next.

This module specifies a simple Markov-style probabilistic transition system encoded in TLA+ using rational weights represented as numerator-denominator tuples. The state starts at an initial node and evolves according to a transition function, while the variable p accumulates path probability mass by multiplying the current probability tuple by the chosen transition weight. The specification defines initialization, a next-state relation with weak fairness, and proves that every behavior satisfying Spec eventually reaches an accepting state or a zero-normalized probability.

This module specifies a very simple system in which a single variable x starts at 0 and is repeatedly incremented by 2 forever. The file includes a PlusCal algorithm and its generated TLA+ translation, with the temporal specification given by Init /\ [][Next]_vars. It proves a type invariant that x always remains a natural number and also proves that x is always even, using TLAPS proof steps and the auxiliary divisibility operator a|b.

This module specifies and proves correctness of a very simple algorithm for finding the largest value in a sequence of natural numbers. The algorithm iterates through a sequence variable f, maintains a current highest value h, and advances an index i until termination, after which h is shown to be greater than or equal to every element of the sequence. The specification includes the PlusCal algorithm and its TLA+ translation, defines type and inductive invariants, proves a helper property about the final index value, and then proves overall correctness with TLAPS proof steps. The design explicitly allows infinite stuttering after termination to avoid deadlock.

This module specifies and model checks an implementation of Booth's algorithm for finding the lexicographically least circular substring, i.e. the least rotation of a sequence. The file contains a PlusCal algorithm and its generated TLA+ translation, with state variables tracking the input sequence, its length, the failure-function array, loop indices, and the program counter. It verifies a type invariant over the translated state and states a partial-correctness property asserting that when the program counter reaches "Done", the computed shift k yields a lexicographically minimal rotation, with ties broken by the smallest shift.

This module is a small model-checking wrapper around a least-circular-substring specification. It introduces two constants, one bounding the character set size and one bounding the maximum string length, and then defines finite ranges derived from those constants for use as model domains. The file does not define any state variables, actions, temporal specification, or correctness properties; it only provides simple value-level definitions intended to constrain or instantiate the imported algorithm.

This module defines utility operators for finite zero-indexed sequences represented as functions with domain 0..(n-1). It provides constructors and conversions between ordinary one-indexed TLA+ sequences and this zero-indexed representation, along with derived operators for length, valid indices, rotations, and a lexicographic order. The module is a pure mathematical helper library with no state variables, no transition system, no fault model, and no temporal verification properties; its notable design choice is to represent zero-indexed sequences explicitly as functions rather than using the built-in Sequences indexing convention.

This module specifies the level-checking for the TLA+ language. It defines semantic-node structures, level metadata, and recursive correctness conditions used to determine when expressions are level-correct.

This module specifies a binary search algorithm over a sorted sequence `seq` of integer values from a constant set `Values`, searching for a target value `val`. The translated algorithm maintains variables `low`, `high`, and `result`, repeatedly checking the middle element and narrowing the search range until either a matching index is found or the search terminates with `result = 0`. The specification includes a temporal behavior `Spec` with weak fairness on `Next`, a termination property stating that eventually `pc = "Done"`, and a TLAPS proof that the safety property `resultCorrect` is invariant under the behavior.

This module is a lightweight wrapper around another specification, Majority, and provides Apalache-oriented type annotations plus a concrete value definition for use with configuration. It declares the constants and variables expected by the imported Majority instance and defines a concrete set of values.

This module specifies Boyer and Moore's majority vote algorithm over an input sequence of values. The algorithm scans the sequence in one pass, maintaining an index i, a current candidate cand, and a counter cnt, and it guarantees that when the scan is complete, any value with an absolute majority must equal cand. The specification includes a temporal behavior Spec with initialization, a next-state action, and weak fairness for Next, and it also defines correctness and an inductive invariant used for reasoning about the algorithm.

This module is a thin wrapper around another specification, Reachable, used to attach Apalache type annotations while keeping the original module free of tool-specific annotations. It declares constants for a graph-like structure consisting of a set of nodes, a successor function from nodes to sets of nodes, and a distinguished root node, and it declares variables marked, vroot, and pc with annotated types. The module does not define its own transition system, temporal specification, or correctness properties; instead, it instantiates Reachable with direct substitutions for the three constants and additionally defines concrete constant values NodesVal, SuccVal, and RootVal for use by configuration.

This module contains TLAPS proofs for the safety properties of the parallel reachability algorithm specified in the imported module ParReach. It proves that the invariant Inv is preserved by Spec and also proves a refinement-style safety result showing that the concrete specification implies the initialization and step relation of an instantiated module R under the refinement mapping already defined in ParReach. The file is proof-oriented rather than algorithm-defining: it introduces no new state variables or transition operators of its own, and focuses on invariant preservation, stuttering-step reasoning, and refinement of safety behavior.

This module specifies a parallel multiprocess version of Misra's reachability algorithm. It models a set of processes that cooperatively explore nodes reachable from a distinguished root, maintaining a shared set `marked` and work set `vroot`, with per-process local variables `u` and `toVroot`; the algorithm terminates iff the reachable set from `Root` is finite, and on termination `marked` equals that reachable set. The specification includes the PlusCal translation, a fairness-based temporal specification for all processes, an inductive invariant used for refinement, and theorems asserting that the parallel algorithm refines the imported reachability specification and satisfies both its safety and fairness parts.

This module specifies reachability in a directed graph represented by a set of nodes and a successor function Succ mapping each node to the set of its outgoing neighbors. It defines what it means for a sequence to be a path from one node to another, uses existential quantification over sequences of nodes to define when a path exists, and then defines the set of nodes reachable from a given set S. The module includes a typing assumption that Succ is a function from Nodes to subsets of Nodes, and it contains no state variables, actions, temporal behavior, fairness conditions, or proofs beyond the commented note about TLAPS modules.

This module specifies Jayadev Misra's algorithm for computing the set of graph nodes reachable from a distinguished node Root in a directed graph. The graph structure itself is taken from the imported Reachability module via the constants Nodes and Succ, and the algorithm maintains two sets, marked and vroot, plus a control variable pc generated by the PlusCal translation. The specification defines the translated PlusCal algorithm, its temporal specification with weak fairness of Next, several state invariants used for partial correctness, a theorem asserting that termination implies the computed set equals the mathematical reachable set, and a liveness theorem asserting eventual termination when the reachable set is finite.

This TLA+ specification provides a TLAPS proof for the Missionaries and Cannibals problem, focusing on type correctness. The proof shows that the system, as defined by the Init and Next operators (from the MissionariesAndCannibals module), maintains the TypeOK invariant throughout all behaviors. The property Spec => []TypeOK is proven, where Spec is defined as Init /\ [][Next]_vars. The proof is structured hierarchically and demonstrates that all reachable states satisfy the type invariant, though the comments note that this is not a real safety property but rather a proof skeleton for illustration.

This specification models the classic moving-cat puzzle with a line of numbered boxes. A cat occupies one box and must move every step to an adjacent box without wrap-around, while the observer checks boxes according to a back-and-forth search pattern over boxes 2 through N - 1, reversing direction at the ends. The spec defines an initial state, a cat movement action, an observation action, a combined next-state relation, a temporal specification with weak fairness for the cat's movement, and an eventual victory property stating that the observed box will eventually coincide with the cat's box.

This module contains TLAPS-checked proofs for the multi-car elevator specification, focusing on safety properties. It proves that the system maintains type correctness and safety invariants, as specified in the main Elevator module, by strengthening the state invariant and deriving the required invariants as corollaries. The liveness (temporal) properties are not addressed here. The proofs handle the limitations of TLAPS regarding multi-argument function application by explicitly stating unfolding lemmas, and they make explicit the disjointness between Elevator and Floor, which is implicit in TLC models. The proof strategy involves mutual induction over several auxiliary invariants, with detailed case analysis for each action, but the full inductive step for the strengthened safety invariant is omitted as it is complex and left for future work.

This specification models a simple multi-car elevator system with a set of people, a set of elevators, and a bounded set of floors. It defines how people choose destinations, call elevators, enter and exit cars, how elevators open and close doors, move, stop, and are dispatched to calls using a simple nearest-eligible-elevator policy rather than a globally optimized scheduling algorithm. The specification includes type and safety invariants, temporal liveness expectations that calls are eventually serviced and waiting people eventually reach their destinations, and fairness assumptions over the main actions; it culminates in a theorem asserting that under Spec, the type, safety, and temporal invariants always hold.

This specification models MultiPaxos in the style of state machine replication (SMR) for a single key, supporting both write and read commands. The network is modeled as a monotonic set of sent messages, capturing asynchronous, non-Byzantine behavior: messages may be delayed, duplicated, or lost (with the assumption that lost messages are retried until received). The spec checks linearizability from the client's perspective by observing the sequence of request and acknowledgement events, and verifies liveness by ensuring no deadlocks occur until all requests are observed. The design is modular, with clear separation of client events, server states, and message types, and is implemented in PlusCal with a translation to TLA+ for model checking. Notable design decisions include the use of unique ballots for leader election, explicit modeling of majority quorums, and a focus on practical system behaviors such as idempotency and efficient state space reduction.

This module specifies the N-queens problem and an iterative algorithm that computes all valid queen placements on an N x N chessboard. A placement is represented as a sequence or function from rows to columns, and the specification defines when two queens attack each other, what it means for a partial or full placement to be a solution, and the full set of solutions. The file contains a PlusCal algorithm and its TLA+ translation, with variables tracking partial solutions still to explore and full solutions already found, and it verifies safety properties such as type correctness and solution inclusion as well as temporal properties including termination and weak fairness-based progress.

This module specifies the N-queens problem and an iterative algorithm for computing all solutions. A queen placement is represented as a function from rows to columns, concretely as a sequence, and partial placements are represented as shorter sequences. The algorithm maintains a set of partial solutions in todo and a set of complete solutions in sols, repeatedly extending one partial solution by placing the next queen in every non-attacking column. The specification includes an initial condition, a next-state action with weak fairness, a type invariant, a correctness invariant relating sols and the mathematical set of all solutions, and a termination property asserting that eventually todo becomes empty.

This module adapts an underlying Nano specification to make it amenable to TLC model checking. It introduces a model-level hash function state and a helper implementation of hash calculation so that hash assignment can be represented with finite state, and it adds a stuttering action to stop progress gracefully once available hashes are exhausted. The specification verifies safety-related properties by asserting that the overall behavior satisfies both a type invariant and the underlying Nano safety invariant, while using a view that ignores hashFunction and lastHash when hashing states for model checking.

This module models an early, now-outdated version of the Nano blockchain protocol. It represents signed blocks, account chains, balances, and per-node ledgers, along with actions for creating and processing genesis, open, send, receive, and change-representative blocks. The specification assumes abstract cryptographic primitives for hashing and signatures, models a distributed setting where each node maintains its own ledger and a set of received-but-unprocessed blocks, and verifies a safety theorem showing that the temporal specification implies the type invariant and a cryptographic safety invariant.

This module is an Apalache-oriented wrapper around another TLA+ specification named Prisoner, providing type annotations and a concrete constant value definition used by configuration. It models the constants and variables relevant to a prisoner problem, including a prisoner set, a light state, a count, an announced flag, a per-prisoner signalling function, and a set of prisoners who have visited. The module itself does not define the system dynamics, actions, or temporal properties; instead, it instantiates the Prisoner module and adds a concrete set of prisoner string values for use by APPrisoner.cfg.

This specification models a fair solution to the classic readers-writers problem using a waiting queue of pending access requests. Processes can request either read or write access, queued requests are served from the head of the queue, readers may coexist, and writers require exclusive access with no current readers. The spec defines initialization, state transitions, weak fairness conditions for all request and service actions, safety invariants about mutual exclusion and writer cardinality, and liveness properties asserting that every actor eventually repeatedly reads, writes, and also eventually leaves those states.

This specification models an improved Software Defined Perimeter (SDP) architecture with a legitimate client, an SDP controller, a firewall, a target server, and an attacker operating under a Dolev-Yao-style attacker model for message interception, replay, spoofing, and probing. The design ties SPA authentication sessions to concrete data-plane TCP connection attempts using encrypted client/server tuple information, and the firewall is configured with exact 4-tuple ACL rules after successful authentication. The spec verifies both safety and liveness-style temporal properties about SPA authentication, anti-replay and anti-spoof behavior, legitimate user access availability, server hiddenness against attackers, firewall rule consistency, and firewall correctness under retransmission scenarios.

This specification models a Software Defined Perimeter (SDP) architecture with a legitimate client, an SDP controller, a firewall, a target server, and an attacker. The client performs Single Packet Authorization (SPA), the controller authenticates SPA messages and installs firewall ACL rules, the firewall mediates data-plane TCP traffic, and the attacker can sniff, replay, spoof, and probe based on captured information under a Dolev-Yao style threat model that does not break the underlying crypto abstractions. The spec verifies both safety and liveness-style properties, including that attacker SPA attempts are detected, legitimate SPA sessions lead to corresponding ACL rules, legitimate user access can eventually succeed, firewall behavior is consistent, and the attacker should not successfully establish protected service access.

This module provides Apalache-specific type annotations and concrete constant-value helper definitions for an underlying single-lane bridge specification. It declares the constant sets for cars approaching from the right and left, the bridge positions, and the overall positions domain, and it declares state variables for car locations and the queue of cars waiting before the bridge. The module instances the separate SingleLaneBridge specification module, but this file itself only contains the declarations, the instance statement, and concrete value definitions; it does not define the transition relation, temporal specification, or fault model directly.

This specification models traffic over a single-lane bridge where cars may travel in two opposite directions, represented by the disjoint sets CarsRight and CarsLeft. The bridge admits concurrent movement only for cars traveling in the same direction, and the specification enforces safety conditions preventing cars going in opposite directions from occupying the bridge simultaneously or colliding within bridge positions. The model defines movement, waiting behavior before entering the bridge, weak fairness assumptions for movement and entry actions, and verifies safety invariants, typing constraints, and liveness properties stating that cars eventually enter and eventually exit the bridge.

This module specifies the Slush protocol, a simple consensus algorithm from the Avalanche family, using a PlusCal algorithm translated into TLA+. The model captures nodes that hold colors, loop processes that repeatedly query sampled peers, query processes that answer with their current color, and a client process that initially assigns colors to uncolored nodes. The comments explicitly note that the protocol is probabilistic in intent, but the TLA+ model is not probabilistic and is therefore mainly useful as executable pseudocode plus basic temporal checking. The specification defines an initial state, a next-state relation over the translated PlusCal control flow, a type invariant, and a temporal termination property asserting eventual completion of all processes. It also includes an explicit terminating stuttering action to avoid deadlock once all processes reach the Done control state.

This specification models a spanning-tree construction algorithm over an arbitrary graph whose node set is fixed by the constant Nodes and whose edge set is chosen nondeterministically as an initial value of the variable Edges. Each node maintains a parent pointer mom and an estimated distance dist from the distinguished root Root; nodes repeatedly update their parent and distance when they discover a neighbor with a shorter path, choosing any improved distance strictly between the neighbor's distance plus one and the node's current distance minus one. The spec checks type correctness, defines a temporal specification with weak fairness on Next, and states safety and liveness properties including a postcondition characterizing rooted, unreachable, and reachable nodes as well as an additional property AllDistancesOne.

This module provides a TLAPS proof that the SpanTree specification guarantees the type invariant TypeOK is always maintained. The proof shows that if the initial state satisfies TypeOK and every step of the Next action preserves TypeOK, then the temporal property []TypeOK holds under the given specification Spec. The proof assumes certain properties about the constants, such as Root being a node, every edge being a subset of Nodes of cardinality 2, and MaxCardinality being a natural number at least as large as the number of nodes. The proof is structured hierarchically and uses standard TLAPS proof commands.

This module defines a small library of TLA+ operators for representing BNF-style grammars as languages over sequences of strings. It includes constructors for singleton-sequence languages, concatenation, union, one-or-more repetition, zero-or-more repetition, a grammar type as a function from strings to sets of string sequences, and a least-grammar operator defined with CHOOSE. The module has no constants, variables, actions, temporal formulas, assumptions, or PlusCal code.

This module provides a formalization of differential equations and their solutions in TLA+. It defines what it means for a function to be a first derivative (IsFirstDeriv) and recursively defines higher-order derivatives (IsDeriv). The Integrate operator expresses the existence and construction of a solution to an n-th order ordinary differential equation with given initial values, using a choice function to select a suitable solution. The module uses real numbers and sequences, and encodes open intervals and neighborhoods for analysis, but does not specify a particular algorithm or system beyond these mathematical definitions.

This module defines basic graph-theoretic structures and properties in TLA+. It models both directed and undirected graphs as records with node and edge fields, and provides predicates for checking if a structure is a directed or undirected graph. The module also defines subgraph constructions, paths, connectivity, and rooted trees, using set and sequence operations. No temporal properties or fault models are present; the focus is on static graph properties and relationships.

This specification models an inner sequential memory/request handling component with per-process register files, a per-process queue of issued operations, and a memory array. Processes can issue requests into free registers, receive responses for reads and writes, and internally remove completed operations from the head of their queue, updating memory for writes and checking consistency for reads. The spec asserts a data invariant over the register file, operation queues, and memory structure, and defines a temporal specification with weak fairness for response actions and queue removal so that enabled operations are not postponed forever.

This specification models an inner serial memory/register interface that tracks per-process sequences of issued operations, their responses, and a partial order over operation identifiers. It distinguishes read and write requests, records the source write that supplies a read value, and constrains the evolving order relation so that the completed history is serializable by extension to some total order consistent with program order and read-from constraints. The spec initializes empty operation queues, allows issuing requests, responding to reads and writes, and internal steps that only extend the order relation, and it verifies the system with a temporal specification using weak fairness for response actions and for internal ordering steps that eventually compare distinct operations.

This module defines the interface-level data types and type invariant for a register file. It models read requests, write requests, and free register values as record-shaped values over the constant sets Adr, Val, Proc, and Reg, and then combines them into larger sets used to constrain the state variable regFile. The specification does not define an initial condition, transition relation, or temporal behavior; instead, it provides structural type definitions and a state invariant asserting that regFile maps each process to a mapping from registers to register-interface values.

This module defines a serial memory specification by existentially quantifying over an initial memory state and two auxiliary values, then delegating the actual behavior to the `Spec` operator of an instantiated `InnerSerial` module. The initial memory is constrained to be a function from addresses to values, while `opQ` and `opOrder` are existentially chosen. The module is a thin wrapper around another module instance and does not itself define actions, fairness, assumptions, or proofs.

This module provides a TLAPS proof of the main theorem from AsynchInterface.tla, which asserts that the specification Spec implies that the type invariant TypeInvariant is always maintained. The proof is structured hierarchically and uses TLAPS proof commands and references to definitions from the AsynchInterface module. The proof demonstrates type correctness for the asynchronous interface protocol, focusing on the preservation of the type invariant across the system's transitions. The module does not introduce new operators or variables, but rather proves properties about those defined in the extended module.

This module provides a TLAPS proof of the main theorem from Channel.tla, which asserts that the specification Spec implies that the type invariant TypeInvariant is always maintained. The proof is structured hierarchically and uses TLAPS proof commands and backend solvers. The module does not define any new operators or variables, but instead proves a property about the system specified in the Channel module.

This module provides a TLAPS proof for the InternalMemory specification, specifically proving that the type invariant (TypeInvariant) is preserved by the system. The proof addresses the fact that TypeInvariant alone is not inductive due to the next-state expression in Do(p) accessing fields of buf[p] that are only valid when buf[p] is in MReq. To resolve this, the invariant is strengthened with BufConsistent, which ensures that buf[p] has the correct type depending on the value of ctl[p]. The main theorem proved is that ISpec implies the temporal property []TypeInvariant, with the proof structured hierarchically and using TLAPS proof commands.

This module specifies an internal memory component that interacts with an external memory interface through request and reply actions. It models a small protocol in which each process moves through control states "rdy", "busy", and "done", stores either requests or returned values in a per-process buffer, and updates the memory state on write requests while returning a memory value on reads. The specification defines an initial condition, a next-state relation over per-process actions, a temporal specification using a stuttering-closed box action, and proves that the type invariant always holds.

This module specifies a simple memory interface vocabulary rather than a full transition system. It defines the shape of memory requests as either read requests with an address or write requests with an address and value, and it defines a distinguished value NoVal chosen to lie outside the set Val. The file declares an interface variable and several constants for send/reply relations, initialization, and basic domains, but it does not define an Init, Next, Spec, or temporal correctness property. A commented-out assumption indicates the intended typing of Send and Reply as boolean-valued operators over process, data, and old/new memory-interface states, but because it is commented out it is not part of the active syntax.

This module defines a very small wrapper specification for a memory system by instantiating another module named InternalMemory with parameters mem, ctl, and buf. It extends MemoryInterface and defines an operator Inner that is an INSTANCE of InternalMemory, then defines Spec existentially over the instance parameters and refers to the instantiated specification ISpec. The file contains no state variables, no actions defined locally, and no explicit temporal properties beyond the top-level Spec expression that delegates behavior to the instantiated module.

This specification models a write-through cache system layered over an internal memory interface, with the original module instantiation expanded manually because the TLC version targeted by the file could not handle INSTANCE. The system has per-processor control state, request buffers, a per-processor cache, and a memory request queue that serializes cache misses and writes to memory. It specifies initialization, state-transition actions for requests, reads, writes, queue processing, and eviction, and it asserts temporal safety properties that the type invariant and cache coherence hold under the main specification.

This specification models a write-through cache layered over an internal memory interface. It describes per-processor cache behavior, request and response handling, read misses, writes that update both cache state and a memory queue, queued memory processing, and eviction. The spec verifies a type invariant and a cache coherence property stating that if two cached values for the same address are both valid, then they are equal; it also proves refinement or conformance to an instantiated Memory specification.

This specification models a binary hour clock in which the variable bits represents an array of binary digits encoding an hour value. The module defines a helper operator to interpret a bit array as a numeric value, then relates that interpreted value to an hour variable through a temporal invariant stating that the hour always equals the value computed from bits. The top-level formula existentially quantifies an hour variable and combines that relation with the imported HourClock instance's HC property, so the design connects a binary representation of hours to an abstract hour-clock specification.

This specification models a refinement relationship between two channel instances, a low-level bit channel and a high-level channel carrying values in 1..12. The inner module introduces a state variable bitsSent and accumulates up to three transmitted bits, converting a completed bit sequence into a natural number with BitSeqToNat and forwarding it on the high-level channel. It also models an error behavior in which the low-level channel changes unexpectedly while no send or receive is occurring, forcing the high-level channel state to ErrorVal; the temporal properties define the inner behavior and then existentially hide bitsSent to obtain the overall refinement formula IR.

This module provides a TLAPS proof of the main theorem from Channel.tla, which asserts that the specification Spec implies that the type invariant TypeInvariant is always maintained. The proof is structured hierarchically and uses TLAPS proof commands and backend solvers. The system being modeled is a channel, and the proof demonstrates type correctness under the specified actions and invariants.

This specification models a simple two-phase handshake communication channel using a single variable 'chan' that is a record with fields 'val', 'rdy', and 'ack'. The channel transmits values from the set 'Data' using a protocol where the sender updates the value and toggles the ready bit, and the receiver acknowledges by toggling the ack bit. The system ensures that the channel variable always satisfies the type invariant, and the main temporal property asserts that this invariant is always maintained throughout execution. The model is basic, with no explicit fault model or fairness conditions, and verifies safety via a single theorem.

This specification models a composite FIFO-style communication system built by connecting a sender, an inner buffer, and a receiver through channel interfaces. The top-level module instantiates a Channel module twice, once for the input side and once for the output side, and also defines an inner module that represents a queue-based buffer with receive and send actions over those channels. The specification asserts structural channel constraints on the records in and out, constrains acknowledgement and ready fields to match, and composes the Sender, existentially quantified Buffer, and Receiver behaviors into the overall Spec; it does not include explicit fault modeling or proof scripts.

This module provides a TLAPS proof of a theorem about the HourClock specification, specifically that the invariant HCini is preserved by the system. The proof shows that if HC holds, then HCini holds always, using the temporal property []HCini. The proof is structured hierarchically and references definitions from the HourClock module, with fairness and next-state actions handled via [HCnxt]_hr.

This specification models a simple 12-hour clock. The state variable 'hr' represents the current hour, which ranges from 1 to 12. The initial predicate HCini ensures that the hour starts within this range, and the next-state action HCnxt increments the hour by 1 unless it is 12, in which case it wraps around to 1. The temporal property HC asserts that the system starts in a valid state and always follows the hour update rule. The theorem verifies that the invariant HCini is always maintained.

This module provides a TLAPS proof for the InternalMemory specification, specifically proving that the type invariant (TypeInvariant) is preserved by the system. The proof addresses the fact that TypeInvariant alone is not inductive due to the next-state expression in Do(p) accessing fields of buf[p] that are only valid when buf[p] is in MReq. To resolve this, the invariant is strengthened with BufConsistent, which ensures that buf[p] has the correct type depending on the value of ctl[p]. The main theorem proved is that ISpec implies []TypeInvariant, with the proof structured hierarchically and using TLAPS proof commands.

This module specifies an internal memory system that implements the MemoryInterface. The system models a set of processes interacting with a shared memory, where each process can issue memory requests, perform operations, and receive responses. The state is tracked by variables for memory contents, control state per process, and a buffer per process. The algorithm ensures that memory operations are performed atomically and that the control and buffer variables are updated consistently. The specification includes a type invariant to ensure variables remain within their intended domains, and a temporal property stating that the type invariant is always preserved by the system. The system interacts with an abstract memory interface via Send and Reply actions, and the fairness and stuttering are handled via the temporal box operator.

This specification models a joint-action memory system by composing two hidden internal components: an environment component and a memory component. The environment tracks a readiness map and can either send memory requests or receive replies, while the memory component accepts requests into per-process buffers, updates control state, and delegates additional behavior to imported operators such as Do and Rsp from an extended module. The top-level specification existentially hides the internal variables of both components and asserts the conjunction of their temporal behaviors, with each component described by an initialization predicate and a stuttering-closed next-state formula.

This module provides a TLAPS proof of the main theorem from Channel.tla, specifically that the specification Spec implies that the type invariant TypeInvariant is always maintained. The proof is structured hierarchically and uses TLAPS proof commands and backend solvers. The module does not define any new operators or variables, but instead focuses on proving the temporal property using the definitions from the Channel module.

This module specifies a simple one-place handshake channel with a data field and two control bits, rdy and ack. The sender may send a value d only when chan.rdy = chan.ack, and doing so stores d in chan.val and flips the ready bit; the receiver may receive only when chan.rdy # chan.ack, and doing so flips the acknowledge bit. The specification defines initialization, the next-state relation, and a temporal behavior Spec asserting Init and always Next over chan, and it proves that the type invariant is always maintained.

This specification defines a top-level FIFO module that declares a constant Message and two variables, in and out. It defines Inner(q) as an instance of InnerFIFO, and defines Spec as \EE q : Inner(q)!Spec. No assumptions, theorems, actions, temporal operators with outermost [] or <>, fairness conditions, proofs, or PlusCal constructs are defined in this file.

This module specifies an inner FIFO buffer system connecting an input channel and an output channel, with an internal queue q storing messages in transit. The module is a TLC-oriented version of another specification that originally used INSTANCE statements; here the imported channel behavior is expanded manually into prefixed operators for the input and output channels. It models channel handshaking with rdy/ack bits, queueing of received input messages, forwarding from the head of the queue to the output channel, and proves that the specification implies a type invariant stating that both channels have the expected record structure and that q is a sequence of Message values.

This module provides a TLAPS proof for the FIFO queue specification defined in the InnerFIFO module. The main theorem proved is that the specification Spec implies that the type invariant TypeInvariant is always maintained, i.e., Spec => []TypeInvariant. The proof is structured hierarchically and relies on the definitions and invariants from the InnerFIFO module, as well as proof automation from TLAPS. The proof demonstrates that the initial state satisfies the invariant and that the invariant is preserved by all possible transitions, including Send, Receive, and stuttering steps.

This module specifies an inner FIFO buffer connected between an input channel and an output channel. It instantiates a separate Channel module twice, once for the input channel and once for the output channel, and models an internal queue q that stores messages received from the input until they are forwarded on the output in first-in first-out order. The specification defines initialization, message sending into the input channel, buffering of received input messages, forwarding from the buffer to the output, receipt from the output channel, a next-state relation over these actions, and a temporal specification asserting that all behaviors start in Init and evolve by Next with stuttering allowed. It also states a theorem that Spec implies the invariant that both channel instances satisfy their type invariants and that q is a sequence of Message values.

This module provides a TLAPS proof for the main invariant theorem of the HourClock specification. It proves that if the HourClock system (HC) holds initially, then the invariant HCini is always maintained throughout the execution. The proof is structured hierarchically and uses TLAPS proof commands and backend solvers. The design is focused on formal verification of the invariant property, leveraging the temporal logic of actions and proof steps.

This module provides a TLAPS proof of a theorem about the HourClock specification, specifically that the invariant HCini is preserved by the system. The proof shows that if HC holds, then HCini holds always, using the temporal property []HCini. The proof is structured hierarchically and references definitions from the HourClock module, with fairness and next-state actions handled via [HCnxt]_hr.

This specification models a simple 12-hour clock. The state variable 'hr' represents the current hour and is constrained to be in the range 1 to 12. The initial predicate HCini ensures that the hour starts within this range. The next-state action HCnxt increments the hour by 1 unless it is 12, in which case it wraps around to 1. The temporal property HC asserts that the system starts in a valid state and always takes valid next steps. The theorem proves that the invariant HCini is always maintained.

This module provides a TLAPS proof for the InternalMemory specification, specifically proving that the type invariant (TypeInvariant) is preserved by the system under the ISpec specification. The proof addresses the fact that TypeInvariant alone is not inductive due to the next-state expression in Do(p) accessing fields of buf[p] that are only valid when buf[p] is in MReq. To resolve this, the invariant is strengthened with BufConsistent, which ensures that buf[p] has the correct type depending on the value of ctl[p]. The proof is structured hierarchically and demonstrates that the strengthened invariant (Inv) is inductive, and thus TypeInvariant is always preserved.

This module specifies an internal memory system that implements the MemoryInterface. The system models a set of processes interacting with a shared memory, where each process can issue memory requests, perform operations, and receive responses. The state is tracked by variables for memory contents (mem), control state per process (ctl), and per-process buffers (buf). The algorithm models request, operation, and response phases for each process, with explicit state transitions and primed variables. The main temporal property ISpec asserts that starting from IInit, the system repeatedly executes INext steps, and a theorem proves that the type invariant is always maintained. The design uses explicit state transitions and does not include a fault model.

This module augments the InternalMemory specification with liveness requirements for the internal memory system. It defines the tuple of variables used for temporal subscripting, introduces two alternative liveness formulas based on weak fairness of processor actions, and then defines LISpec as the original safety specification ISpec conjoined with one of those liveness conditions. The module also states a liveness property saying that whenever a processor's control state is busy, it eventually reaches the ready state, and includes a theorem asserting that LISpec implies this leads-to property.

This module augments a write-through cache specification with liveness conditions. According to the comments, it adds the liveness condition described for the write-through cache and uses an equivalent definition of Spec from the instanced module so that TLC can check it. The module defines fairness requirements over cache response, read, write, and memory-queue actions, including a queue condition based on queue length or the presence of a read request, and then combines these fairness conditions with the imported safety specification.

This module provides a TLAPS proof of a theorem about the HourClock specification, specifically that the invariant HCini is preserved by the HourClock system. The proof shows that if HC holds, then HCini holds always, by proving that HCini is preserved by the next-state relation HCnxt. The proof is structured hierarchically and uses the PTL backend for temporal logic reasoning.

This specification models a simple 12-hour clock. The state variable 'hr' represents the current hour, which ranges from 1 to 12. The initial predicate HCini ensures that hr starts within this range. The next-state action HCnxt increments hr by 1 unless it is 12, in which case it wraps around to 1. The temporal property HC asserts that the system starts in a valid state and always evolves according to HCnxt. The theorem proves that the invariant HCini is always maintained. The design is straightforward, with no fault model or concurrency, and focuses on demonstrating a cyclic counter with a simple temporal invariant.

This module provides a TLAPS proof for the InternalMemory specification, specifically proving that the type invariant (TypeInvariant) is preserved by the system. The proof addresses the fact that TypeInvariant alone is not inductive due to the way the next-state action Do(p) accesses fields of buf[p], which are only valid when buf[p] is in MReq. To resolve this, the invariant is strengthened with BufConsistent, which ensures that buf[p] has the correct type depending on the value of ctl[p]. The main theorem proved is that ISpec implies []TypeInvariant, using the strengthened invariant Inv (TypeInvariant /\ BufConsistent). The proof is structured hierarchically and uses TLAPS proof commands and backend solvers.

This module specifies an internal memory system that implements the MemoryInterface. The system models a set of processes interacting with a shared memory, where each process can issue memory requests, perform operations, and receive responses. The state is tracked by variables for memory contents (mem), control state per process (ctl), and per-process buffers (buf). The algorithm models request, operation, and response phases for each process, with explicit state transitions and primed variables. The specification asserts a type invariant is always maintained, and the main temporal property (ISpec) requires that the system starts in a valid initial state and all steps follow the allowed transitions, with the type invariant holding globally. The design uses explicit state transitions and does not model faults or failures.

This module specifies a simple real-time framework with a single clock variable now ranging over a bounded set of natural-number time values from 0 to MaxReal. It defines an initialization predicate for time, a real-time next-state relation RTNext(v) that either advances time while keeping an auxiliary state component v unchanged or keeps time fixed while allowing v to change, and a timer transition rule TimerNext that updates a timer variable t based on whether an action A occurs or is disabled. The specification also defines a fairness condition RTFairness(v) requiring weak fairness of time-progress steps above every real threshold, but it does not define a complete top-level Spec operator in this file.

This specification defines a real-time memory-related wrapper around an internal memory specification. The top-level module introduces a positive real-time bound constant Rho, defines an inner module in which a response action forces a process control state to become "rdy", and requires that every process satisfy a real-time bound RTBound on that response action together with the imported internal-memory specification ISpec. The top-level property RTSpec existentially quantifies the internal state variables mem, ctl, and buf and states that there exists an instance of the inner real-time internal-memory specification satisfying RTISpec; the file uses imported real-time operators but does not itself define transition-system variables or proofs.

This module defines a real-time wrapper around an existing write-through cache specification. It extends the underlying cache model with an additional variable lastP and a scheduling discipline that uses a computed position order to control which process may take certain expensive actions, specifically read misses and writes, while preserving other cache and memory queue actions. The specification assumes real-time parameters Delta, Epsilon, and Rho are positive reals satisfying a timing bound, and it asserts a real-time temporal specification RTSpec that combines initialization, a next-state relation, bounded-response timing constraints via RTBound, and the RTnow clocking condition; it finally states a theorem that this real-time specification implies the instantiated RTMemory real-time specification.

This specification models a real-time hour clock by combining a real-valued time variable with an underlying hour-clock module. The outer module introduces a continuously increasing real-valued variable now and assumes a positive timing tolerance constant Rho; an inner module defines a timer variable t that is reset when the underlying hour clock advances and otherwise accumulates elapsed real time. The specification asserts timing bounds showing that the hour clock advances no later than 3600 + Rho seconds and, when it advances, no earlier than 3600 - Rho seconds, and the top-level behavior combines the inherited hour-clock behavior, monotonic real time, and the existence of an inner timer instance satisfying these real-time constraints.

This module defines real-time temporal constraints over actions by introducing an explicit real-valued time variable `now` and auxiliary timer behavior. The operator `RTBound(A, v, D, E)` specifies that there exists a timer `t` which is reset when action `A` occurs or when `A` becomes disabled in the next state, otherwise advances by the elapsed real time `now' - now`, while also enforcing an upper bound `E` and a lower bound `D` relative to occurrences of `A`. The operator `RTnow(v)` constrains `now` to range over the reals, to increase monotonically through a stuttering-insensitive next-state action `NowNext`, and adds a weak fairness condition ensuring time can always progress past any real threshold.

This module defines a standard TLA+ representation of bags (multisets) as functions from elements to positive natural numbers, where the domain contains exactly the elements present in the bag and the function value gives the multiplicity. It provides operators for recognizing bags, converting between sets and bags, bag membership, empty bags, bag union and difference, subbag comparison, the set of all subbags, image construction over bags, cardinality, and counting copies of an element. The module is a pure mathematical library module rather than a transition-system specification: it has no variables, actions, or temporal properties, and its comments note that most operators are overridden by TLC except for SubBag.

This module defines the standard finite-set operators `IsFiniteSet` and `Cardinality`. It characterizes finiteness by the existence of a finite sequence whose elements cover the set, and it defines cardinality recursively over subsets by removing one chosen element at a time until the empty set is reached. The file contains no state variables, no actions, and no temporal specification; it is a pure mathematical utility module with comments explaining that TLC overrides these operators in Java.

This module is a dummy replacement for the standard TLA+ Integers module. It extends Naturals and provides placeholder definitions for integer-related operators, with comments explaining that tools such as TLC are expected to override these definitions with real implementations. The module defines the integer set Int as the empty set and defines the prefix negation operator in terms of subtraction, serving as a structural specification stub rather than a complete algorithmic system.

This module is a dummy placeholder specification for the standard Naturals module rather than an algorithm or distributed system. It defines placeholder versions of natural-number-related operators such as arithmetic, comparisons, and ranges, with comments explaining that real tools are expected to override them with proper implementations. The file contains no state variables, no transition system, no temporal behavior, no fault model, and no verified safety or liveness properties; its notable design decision is that most operators are given trivial or symbolic definitions solely as stand-ins.

This module axiomatizes the Peano natural numbers using three parameters: a carrier set N, a distinguished zero element Z, and a successor function Sc. The main operator PeanoAxioms states that zero is in N, successor maps N to N, every non-zero element is the successor of some element, and every subset of N containing zero and closed under successor is all of N. The module then assumes existence of such a structure and defines Succ, Nat, and Zero by CHOOSE expressions to extract a particular successor function, its domain as the naturals, and a corresponding zero element.

This module axiomatizes and then selects a model of the real numbers on top of a Peano-style natural-number foundation imported from the Peano module. It defines a predicate IsModelOfReals(R, Plus, Times, Leq) expressing algebraic, order, and completeness properties of a real-number structure, proves existentially that some such model exists, then chooses one witness RM and introduces derived operators for Real numbers, infinities, arithmetic, ordering, subtraction, division, integers, and exponentiation. The specification is not a transition-system or fault-tolerant protocol model; instead it is a mathematical TLA+ theory module with no variables, no actions, and no temporal behavior, focused on abstract construction and characterization of reals and extended-real-like values.

This module provides placeholder definitions for real-number-related operators rather than a full executable semantics. It models a dummy Reals module by defining a distinguished value Real, division as a CHOOSE-based operator over that value, and Infinity as a CHOOSE of an element outside Real that is greater than every element of Real. The file does not define a transition system, state variables, actions, temporal specification, fairness, or proofs; it is a mathematical support module intended for use by other specifications and tools.

This module defines standard operators for finite sequences in TLA+, representing a sequence of length n as a function with domain 1..n. It provides constructors and selectors such as Seq, Len, concatenation, Append, Head, Tail, SubSeq, and SelectSeq, with comments explaining their intended meaning and the representation of tuples as sequences. The module is a library-style definitions module rather than a transition-system specification: it declares no variables, no actions, and no temporal properties, and it notes that TLC overrides these operators with Java implementations.

This module defines a grammar for the TLA+ language itself using grammar-combinator style operators imported from other modules. It defines lexical classes, operator-token classes, and a parameterized grammar operator P inside TLAPlusGrammar, then returns LeastGrammar(P). It is not a state-machine specification and contains no variables, actions, or temporal correctness properties.

This module provides a TLAPS proof of type correctness for the Alternating Bit protocol, as specified in AlternatingBit.tla. The main theorem proved is that the specification ABSpec implies that the type invariant ABTypeInv always holds. The proof is structured hierarchically, with supporting lemmas establishing the type preservation of sequence operations such as Append, Tail, and Head, as well as the correctness of the Lose operation. The proof uses standard TLAPS commands and relies on the AlternatingBit and TLAPS modules for definitions and proof infrastructure.

This module specifies the alternating bit protocol as a simple sender-receiver communication system with separate message and acknowledgment queues. The sender keeps a data value and a control bit, retransmits when an acknowledgment has not yet matched the current bit, and the receiver records the last received bit and data value while sending acknowledgments back. The environment may nondeterministically lose one element from either queue, and the specification checks a type invariant over the protocol state under a temporal specification with weak fairness for retransmission and acknowledgment sending and strong fairness for message and acknowledgment receipt.

This module defines a grammar for TLA+ configuration files using operators from the BNFGrammars module. It characterizes lexical classes such as letters, digits, identifiers, keywords, strings, and numbers, and then builds a grammar for configuration statements like SPECIFICATION, INIT, NEXT, VIEW, SYMMETRY, constraints, properties, constant replacements, and constant assignments. The specification is purely structural and declarative: it introduces no state variables, no transition actions, and no temporal correctness properties, but instead defines the accepted syntax of config files via grammar combinators and a LET-local grammar parameterized operator.

This specification models a state-graph exploration algorithm that searches a directed graph represented as a record with components `states`, `initials`, and `actions`. The explorer does not enforce BFS ordering: the frontier `S` is a set, and the next state to explore is chosen non-deterministically, while it still records predecessor edges and level information to reconstruct a counterexample path. It checks for safety violations and deadlocks, reconstructs a path once termination is detected, and asserts temporal properties for overall termination and for eventual discovery of a violation state together with a valid counterexample path, under weak fairness of `Next`.

This module defines a collection of directed state graphs together with associated violation sets and example counterexample paths, intended for testing model-checker specifications such as TLCMC and MCReachability. Each graph is represented as a record with fields for the set of states, the set of initial states, and a sequence of successor-state sets indexed by state number; separate operators define the corresponding violating states and witness traces. The module contains no variables, actions, temporal specification, fairness, or proofs; instead it serves as a static data library that selects one named test case based on the IO environment variable GRAPH, defaulting to graph 7 when that setting is absent.
