This module models a TLC-like reachability model checker that performs breadth-first exploration over a graph of states, with a parameter K controlling whether exploration is strict BFS (K = 1) or degraded non-strict BFS (K > 1) to approximate multiple workers. The state graph is given as a record with states, initial states, and an action relation, and the model checker tracks explored states, a queue of pending states, predecessor information, and BFS levels in order to detect violations and reconstruct counterexamples. The specification verifies termination of the translated PlusCal algorithm and a liveness-style property stating that when violation states exist, the eventual counterexample belongs to a supplied set of known counterexamples, with an additional minimal-length requirement when K = 1; it also includes a refinement mapping to an instantiated MCReachability specification.

This module provides wrapper theorems that expose TypeOK and Inv as named invariants of the Spec for the SimpleRegular algorithm. The actual inductive content and algorithmic details are contained in the imported SimpleRegular module; this file focuses on stating and proving that TypeOK and Inv are invariants under the system's specification. The proofs are structured hierarchically and use TLAPS proof constructs, but do not introduce new algorithmic content or state variables. The design is intended for proof management and clarity, making the invariants explicit for use in further verification or as proof obligations.

This module provides wrapper theorems that expose TypeOK and Inv as named invariants of the Spec specification. The actual inductive content and system model are defined in the imported Simple module, specifically in its Correctness property. The theorems here formally state that Spec implies the invariance of TypeOK and Inv, and provide structured proofs using TLAPS proof steps. No algorithm or system is directly modeled in this file; instead, it serves as a proof harness for properties defined elsewhere.

This module specifies a simple alternating system with two state variables, v and x. The variable v acts as a control bit that alternates between 0 and 1, and each transition corresponds to one of two abstract actions: an A_0 action when v changes from 0 to 1, and an A_1 action when v changes from 1 to 0. The details of x's initial value and transition behavior are abstracted by the operator-valued constants XInit and XAct, and the temporal property Spec requires the system to start in Init and then always take Next steps.

This module specifies the two-phase handshake protocol, a fundamental hardware protocol involving a Producer and a Consumer process that alternate actions, with the Producer acting first. The protocol is modeled with variables representing the state of the Producer (p), Consumer (c), and an abstract data variable (x), with actions for each process and a temporal specification ensuring alternation. The module also demonstrates that this protocol implements the Alternate specification under a refinement mapping, using a function vBar to relate the two, and provides a detailed TLAPS proof of this implementation.

This module specifies the Yo-Yo leader election algorithm on arbitrary strongly connected undirected graphs without self-loops, where nodes are identified by integers and the node with the smallest identifier is the eventual leader. The algorithm maintains an orientation of graph edges via incoming and outgoing neighbor sets and alternates between a down phase, where minimum identifiers are propagated toward sinks, and an up phase, where yes/no replies propagate back and edges receiving a "no" are reversed. The specification models asynchronous node steps as a state machine, assumes a strongly connected undirected input graph, and verifies type correctness, structural neighbor consistency, absence of newly created sources, and eventual stabilization to a state where only the minimum node remains the unique source and all up messages are "yes".

This specification models the Yo-Yo leader-election algorithm on a strongly connected undirected graph, extended with pruning so that the algorithm terminates. Nodes alternate between down and up phases, exchange structured messages through mailboxes, reverse or prune edges based on replies, and eventually eliminate all but one source so that the smallest node becomes an isolated leader. The spec assumes a connected undirected graph, uses weak fairness for the main next-state action, and states both safety-style properties about graph consistency and termination-style temporal properties such as eventual termination and equivalence between deadlock and the terminated condition.

This module specifies a non-blocking atomic commitment protocol variant in which reliable broadcast is used to obtain the non-blocking property. It extends a base module for atomic commitment and adds participant forwarding state so that when a participant receives a decision, it forwards that decision to all other participants before locally delivering it. The specification defines participant-side actions for forwarding, pre-deciding from forwarded or coordinator messages, deciding after forwarding is complete, and aborting on simulated timeout conditions, then combines them into a temporal specification with weak fairness assumptions and includes some invalid liveness-style properties such as all-commit, all-abort, and a yes-votes leads-to commit condition.

This module specifies an atomic commitment protocol with one coordinator and a set of participants, using a simple broadcast mechanism in an asynchronous setting. The comments explain that synchronous communication has been replaced by implicit asynchronous communication and that failures are detected magically rather than via timeouts; because broadcast is modeled as a sequence of individual sends that can be interrupted by failure, the protocol is non-terminating and the usual termination property AC5 does not hold. The specification defines typed initial states, participant and coordinator actions, a next-state relation with weak fairness on non-death progress actions, and then states safety, liveness, stronger auxiliary properties, and explicitly invalid properties for the protocol.

This module contains TLAPS proofs for two safety properties of the SimpleAllocator specification: that SimpleAllocator implies the invariants TypeInvariant and ResourceMutex. TypeInvariant is shown to be directly inductive, while ResourceMutex requires the combined invariant Inv (TypeInvariant and ResourceMutex) and an argument about the disjointness of allocated resources. The proofs are fully written in hierarchical style, with detailed reasoning about each action (Request, Allocate, Return) and the preservation of invariants. The module does not define the allocator algorithm itself, but proves properties about it using definitions and actions from the imported SimpleAllocator module.

This module provides a TLAPS proof for the VoucherLifeCycle specification, specifically proving that the temporal property VSpec implies that the invariants VTypeOK and VConsistent always hold. The proof demonstrates that these two invariants together form an inductive invariant for the system. The proof is structured hierarchically and references the underlying system's initialization and next-state actions, but does not introduce new algorithmic behavior or fault models.

This specification models a crash-prone conditional consensus protocol in which processes exchange two phases of broadcast messages and use the maximal proposed value to drive decisions. The fault model is crash failures: up to F processes may crash, and crashed processes stop taking protocol steps. The spec defines initialization, message reception, both broadcast phases, local decision steps, and a deterministic fallback choose step, and it verifies typing, validity, agreement, unconditional termination as a temporal property, and a stronger conditional termination result under Condition1.

This module specifies the Chang-Roberts leader election algorithm on a unidirectional ring of N nodes, where each node has a unique natural-number identity given by the sequence Id. The embedded comments explain that any subset of nodes may initiate the algorithm, and the node with the smallest identity is intended to be elected leader. The specification includes a PlusCal algorithm and its TLA+ translation, defines type correctness and a safety correctness condition about the winner and losing nodes, and states a liveness property that if some candidate exists then eventually some node wins. The temporal specification uses weak fairness for every process action and allows infinite stuttering through a Terminating action to avoid deadlock on termination.

This module defines helper notions on directed acyclic graphs for DAG-based consensus protocols, focusing on vertices that are pairs of a network node and a round. It defines leader vertices, a deterministic-but-arbitrary ordering of set elements, a way to find the previous leader in a DAG, and a recursive linearization procedure that turns a DAG into a sequence. The specification is not itself a full transition-system protocol model with variables and actions; instead it provides structural functions and predicates intended to support safety and liveness reasoning about DAG-based consensus, assuming a genesis vertex and that DAG paths terminate at genesis.

This module defines a directed graph abstraction represented as a pair consisting of a set of vertices and a set of edges. It provides operators to project the vertex and edge components, check whether a value is a well-formed digraph, compute the children of a vertex, compute the descendants reachable from a set of vertices using a recursive definition, and construct the reachable subgraph induced by a starting set of vertices. The module contains no variables, actions, temporal specification, fairness conditions, PlusCal algorithm, or proofs; it is a purely structural and recursive helper module for reasoning about directed graphs.

This module gives a high-level TLA+ specification of the Sailfish and Sailfish++ consensus algorithms, modeling a DAG-based protocol with correct and Byzantine nodes. The comments explain that Byzantine behavior is constrained because vertices are disseminated with reliable broadcast, so Byzantine nodes cannot equivocate and can only create protocol-conforming vertices subject to quorum checks. The specification defines initialization, the next-state relation for correct and Byzantine nodes, a basic type invariant, an agreement safety property over delivered logs, and a liveness property stating that after GST, leaders of synchronous rounds are eventually reflected in correct nodes' logs.

This module defines a small collection of utility operators for use by other specifications. It provides a generic reduction operator over an integer interval, simple arithmetic aggregation, sequence membership and removal helpers, a function range constructor, and a predicate for detecting whether a function induces a simple cycle over a finite set. The module is purely definitional: it declares no variables, no transition actions, and no temporal specification or fault model.

This module specifies an age-aware message channel in which messages are wrapped into boxes that carry both the original message content and an integer-valued transit age. The state tracks the set of boxed messages currently in transit and the set of messages delivered in the current transition, with actions for picking up new messages, delivering a nondeterministically chosen subset addressed to a given receiver, and advancing the age of all in-transit boxes. The specification includes initialization and a type invariant, but it does not define a full temporal specification such as Spec, fairness, or liveness properties; it focuses on the state representation and transition-level behavior of the channel.

This module specifies an eventually perfect failure detector in a partially synchronous distributed system. Each process maintains a local clock, a suspicion set, timeout values for other processes, and counters for how long it has been since it last heard from them; processes periodically send "alive" messages, receive incoming messages supplied by the environment, and periodically predict failures based on timeout expiration. The specification models adaptive timeouts by increasing a timeout when a previously suspected process is heard from again, and it includes a type invariant but no full temporal specification such as Spec, fairness, or liveness properties.

This specification models Dijkstra's first published mutual exclusion algorithm, as described in his 1965 CACM paper. The algorithm ensures mutual exclusion among a set of processes (Proc), each of which cycles through non-critical and critical sections, using shared variables b, c, and k. The PlusCal translation is provided, and the TLA+ translation defines the system's state, actions, and temporal properties. The model checks mutual exclusion, deadlock freedom (under weak fairness), and discusses starvation freedom, with explicit invariants and liveness properties. The design allows for arbitrary process names and includes detailed commentary on the translation and fairness requirements.

This specification models Dijkstra's first published mutual exclusion algorithm for an arbitrary set of processes Proc, using a PlusCal algorithm and its generated TLA+ translation. The system uses shared variables b, c, and k together with per-process control state pc and a temporary local variable temp to represent each process progressing through entry protocol, critical section, and non-critical section. The specification includes the initial condition, next-state relation, and a fairness-based temporal specification Spec, and it defines safety and liveness properties including MutualExclusion, DeadlockFree, StarvationFree, and a stronger DeadlockFreedom property under an alternative liveness specification LSpec.

This module specifies Dijkstra's first published mutual exclusion algorithm, presented as a PlusCal algorithm together with its generated TLA+ translation. It models an arbitrary set Proc of processes that compete to enter a critical section using shared boolean arrays b and c and a shared process-valued variable k, with weak fairness assumptions for process steps in the main specification. The file defines the initial condition, per-control-location actions, the overall next-state relation and specification, and then states safety and liveness properties including mutual exclusion, deadlock freedom, starvation freedom, and a stronger deadlock-freedom property under a modified fairness interpretation.

This module specifies a disk-based variant of Synod/Paxos in which processes interact through persistent disks and maintain local phase, block, and read/write bookkeeping state. The model assumes each process has a disjoint positive ballot set, a distinguished set of disks with a majority predicate, and requires that any two disk majorities intersect. The specification defines initialization, phase-0 recovery reads, phase-1 and phase-2 writes and reads, ballot restarts, and failures, then verifies that the overall behavior refinement-style implies the imported SynodSpec theorem target.

This module augments the DiskSynod specification with additional history variables and inductive invariants for a disk-based Synod/Paxos-style consensus protocol. It introduces `allInput` to track every input value ever seen and `chosen` to record the first non-default output produced by any process, then states a series of higher-level invariants relating ballots, disk blocks, reads, majority sets, and the chosen value. The file does not define a full temporal specification of its own, but instead builds on the imported `Init` and `Next` actions from `DiskSynod` and adds safety-oriented predicates that characterize correctness of the protocol state.

This specification models a simple Synod-style consensus abstraction over a set of processes 1..N, where each process has an input from Inputs and eventually may produce an output. The top-level module introduces an inner module that carries the actual state machine: it initializes each process output to a distinguished non-input value, tracks the set of all current inputs, and allows either a choice step that copies a selected value into an output or a failure-like step that changes a process input. The overall specification hides the internal variables chosen and allInput existentially, and it checks the temporal behavior of the inner system via the invariant-style initialization plus a boxed next-state relation without explicit fairness conditions.

This module specifies the Echo algorithm for constructing a spanning tree in an undirected connected graph starting from a single initiator. The graph is modeled by a set of nodes and a Boolean neighborhood relation R, with assumptions that R is irreflexive, symmetric, and connected; communication is modeled by per-node inbox sets containing message records. The PlusCal algorithm is included together with its TLA+ translation, and the specification verifies safety-style properties such as type correctness, absence of a parent for the initiator, parent-neighbor consistency, parent-child consistency, and ancestor properties at termination, as well as a termination temporal property stating that all processes eventually reach Done.

This module defines basic relational properties and operations for relations represented as binary Boolean functions over a set S. It provides predicates to check if a relation is reflexive, irreflexive, symmetric, asymmetric, transitive, and connected over a set. It also defines operators to compute the transitive closure and reflexive transitive closure of a relation, using recursive LET-bound operators and function constructors. The module is intended as a reusable library for reasoning about relations, and does not specify a particular algorithm or system, nor does it include temporal properties or proofs.

This module specifies the Dijkstra-Scholten distributed termination detection algorithm for a diffusing computation initiated by a distinguished root node. The system maintains a dynamic spanning tree of active nodes, with nodes sending base messages, receiving acknowledgments, detaching from the tree when inactive and childless, and the initiator declaring termination when it becomes inactive and has no remaining children. The specification includes a PlusCal algorithm and its TLA+ translation, models bounded message counts for state-space exploration, assumes a finite node set with an initiator in that set, and verifies both a safety property that termination implies quiescence and a liveness property that quiescence leads to eventual termination under weak fairness of each process action.

This specification models the Dijkstra-Scholten tree algorithm for detecting termination of a diffusing distributed computation over an arbitrary directed process graph. Processes can be active or idle, computation messages flow along graph edges, acknowledgments flow in the reverse direction, and an overlay parent relation is maintained dynamically to form a tree of non-neutral processes rooted at the leader. The spec assumes asynchronous unordered but lossless message delivery, no Byzantine failures, and verifies safety and liveness properties including counter consistency, an overlay-tree invariant, the fact that if the leader is neutral then all other processes are neutral, and the leads-to property that if the computation has terminated then the leader eventually becomes neutral.

This module contains TLAPS proofs for the synchronous termination detection specification defined in the imported module SyncTerminationDetection. It proves safety properties such as type correctness, correctness of termination detection, and quiescence, and also proves a liveness property showing that once the system is terminated and detection has not yet occurred, the DetectTermination action can lead to terminationDetected becoming true. The file is proof-oriented rather than algorithm-defining: it extends the base specification and TLAPS, uses invariance and temporal proof rules, and introduces one lemma characterizing the enabledness of the DetectTermination action.

This module contains TLAPS proofs about a high-level TLA+ specification of asynchronous termination detection. It proves type correctness, safety, stability/quiescence, and a liveness property by reasoning about the imported specification's predicates and actions such as Init, Next, DetectTermination, Terminate, RcvMsg, and SendMsg. The module itself is proof-oriented: it introduces lemmas and theorems over the imported state machine, reduces an ENABLED fairness premise to a state predicate, and uses PTL and ExpandENABLED to discharge temporal reasoning obligations.

This module defines an instrumented and configurable variant of the EWD998 channel-based termination-detection specification for use with TLC trace generation and statistics collection. It adds feature-flag controlled optimizations to token passing, constrains initial simulation states to realistic ones, and defines a behavior specification in which system steps and environment steps evolve under the inherited variables from the base module. The file also configures TLC to run in generation mode, disables deadlock checking because termination is expected, records when termination occurs, and writes per-behavior measurements such as action counts and delay between environment termination and detection to a CSV output.

This module contains TLAPS proofs for the EWD998PCal specification, which is a PlusCal translation of Dijkstra's EWD998 token ring algorithm. In this version, the per-node 'pending' counter and the global 'token' are replaced by a single 'network' variable holding a per-node bag of messages (either payload 'pl' messages or the unique 'tok' message). The refinement mapping recovers the original EWD998 variables from 'network'. The module proves the safety part of the refinement, specifically that the PCal spec refines the original EWD998 spec (Spec => EWD998Spec), focusing on type correctness and the preservation of the unique token property. The proofs include inductive invariants, bag-level reasoning, and per-disjunct case analysis for each possible node action, but the full step-refinement theorem is left as a stub (OMITTED) due to the complexity of the required bag-level lemmas.

This module defines an SVG-based animation layer for Dijkstra's EWD998 distributed termination detection algorithm, specifically for a ring of nodes that exchange messages and circulate a colored token with an accumulated queue count. It is not the base algorithm itself; instead, it extends an existing channel-based specification and visualizes current and next-state information such as node activity, node color, message counters, token position and color, in-flight versus arriving messages, and global status such as running, terminated, or termination detected. The design emphasizes deterministic rendering, modular visual components, debugger watch support, and TLC alias support for frame-by-frame animation generation.

This module is a TLC scripting specification that orchestrates multiple nested TLC runs of another specification, EWD998_opts.tla, in order to collect statistics and write results to a CSV file. It defines a finite set of feature flags and node values, constructs a CSV filename using the current Java time, writes CSV headers, builds a command line for invoking TLC recursively, and then assumes successful execution of nested runs over all subsets of features and all chosen node values. The specification is not modeling the protocol itself directly; instead, it models an experiment driver that uses IO utilities and TLC-side effects to execute simulations and classify outcomes such as assumption, safety, and liveness violations.

This module defines an options and measurement wrapper around the underlying EWD998 termination-detection specification. It introduces feature flags for several algorithm variants, constrains the randomized initial states and environment behavior for TLC generation mode, and defines an alternative system/environment composition used for simulation and data collection. It also records statistics at termination and when termination is detected, using TLC, CSV, and IO utilities, while assuming probabilistic generation mode and disabling deadlock checking because the modeled algorithm is assumed to terminate.

This module defines a generic operator MapThenFoldSet for folding over a set S by first mapping each element x in S through a function f, then combining the results using a binary operator op, starting from a base value. The folding order is determined by a user-supplied choose function, which selects an element from a set; if op is not associative and commutative, the result may depend on the choice order. The comments explain that this is a generalization of simpler fold operators for sets, functions, and sequences, and provide an example usage. No temporal properties or state variables are present; this is a pure functional operator for set processing.

This module defines a collection of operators for reasoning about functions in TLA+, including restriction, range, pointwise operations, inverses, and properties such as injectivity, surjectivity, and bijectivity. It provides definitions for restricting a function to a subset of its domain or to values satisfying a predicate, checking if one function is a restriction of another, and constructing the range of a function. The module also defines operators for constructing sets of injections, surjections, and bijections between sets, as well as checking for their existence. Additional operators include pointwise combination of functions and folding over function values. The module is utility-focused and does not specify a distributed algorithm or system, nor does it include temporal properties or fault models.

This module is a smoke-test harness specification that orchestrates repeated TLC simulations of another specification, SmokeEWD998.tla, and records outcomes to a CSV file. It defines a CSV filename using the current Java time, writes the CSV header at startup via an ASSUME statement, constructs a Java command line for invoking TLC, and then uses a quantified ASSUME to execute many nested runs over combinations of bug flags and random process counts. The module is not itself a transition-system specification with variables or temporal behavior; instead, it is a scripting-style TLA+ model that uses IOUtils, CSV, and TLC operators to drive external execution, classify exit codes such as assumption, invariant, and property violations, and log them.

This module defines a utility predicate for reasoning about finite functional graphs represented by a relation or function r over a set S. The main operator, IsSimpleCycle, characterizes when repeatedly following r from a chosen start node visits exactly the elements of S, using a finite sequence built over 1..Cardinality(S). The module is a helper-style specification with no variables, actions, temporal behavior, fairness, or proofs; it relies on imported modules for integers, sequences, finite-set cardinality, and function-domain/range operators.

This module is a TLAPS proof module for the safety properties of the specification in the extended module clean. It proves that the imported specification Spec implies the invariants []TypeOK, []primerPositive, and []preservationInvariant, and adds an explicit assumption that the unconstrained constants DNA and PRIMER are natural numbers so arithmetic facts can be used in the proofs. The file is proof-oriented rather than algorithm-defining: it contains assumptions, one helper lemma about natMin, and three main theorems with structured proofs over the imported actions heat, cool, anneal, extend, and stuttering via UNCHANGED vars.

This module provides a TLAPS proof of the type-correctness invariant for the system specified in stages.tla. The main property proved is that the type-correctness invariant TypeOK is preserved by the system's specification Spec, i.e., Spec => []TypeOK. The proof is structured hierarchically and checks that all state transitions maintain the Nat-typedness of the relevant variables, using assumptions about the constants and properties of the natMin function. The proof leverages definitions and actions from the extended stages module and uses TLAPS proof commands and structure.

This specification models Lamport's distributed mutual-exclusion algorithm from the 1978 paper "Time, Clocks and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System". It represents a set of processes that communicate by pairwise FIFO message queues, using logical clocks, request messages, acknowledgements, and release notifications to coordinate entry into a critical section. The specification defines the initial state, the process actions for sending and receiving protocol messages, a next-state relation, and a temporal specification `Spec == Init /\\ [][Next]_vars`; it also states safety-oriented predicates such as type correctness, a bounded-network property for model checking, a clock bound state constraint helper, and the mutual exclusion invariant `Mutex`.

This module defines reusable TLA+ operators for adding an auxiliary stuttering variable `s` to an existing specification, as described in the paper "Auxiliary Variables in TLA+". It provides action transformers that wrap an existing subaction `A` with optional pre-stuttering or post-stuttering behavior, using a record-valued control variable `s` whose fields identify the action, its execution context, and a countdown value. The module also defines conditions ensuring that the decrement function driving stuttering eventually reaches a bottom element, including an alternative version intended to be easier for TLC to evaluate on finite models. The file contains no complete system spec of its own; rather, it is a library module meant to be instantiated by another specification, and it includes comments describing a modification that strengthens context checking during stuttering steps.

This module is a TLAPS proof layer for a spanning-tree protocol specification imported from the module spanning. It proves the safety property `Spec => []SntMsg`, where `SntMsg` states that a non-root process whose parent is not yet set has sent no messages. The proof strengthens the invariant with `SentMeansCanSend` and `PrntDomain`, then shows the combined invariant is inductive over `[Next]_vars`; comments also note a design issue in the imported spec's `TypeOK` regarding non-symmetric neighbor relations, so this proof avoids relying on that invariant.

This module specifies a distributed spanning-tree construction over a graph of processes, where processes communicate by recording sent messages in a shared set and adopt a parent when they receive a message. Initially every process has no parent, no process has reported, and no messages have been sent; a process may send to a neighbor if it is the root or it already has a parent, and an unparented non-root process may adopt as parent a sender from which it has received a message. The specification includes a weak fairness condition for the main step relation, a type correctness invariant, a termination property asserting eventual parent assignment for all non-root processes, and a safety-style property stating that once a parent is assigned it never changes.

This module specifies and proves a simple arithmetic fact over natural numbers: for every natural number x, the sum x+x is even. It defines predicates Even and Odd in terms of the remainder modulo 2, then states the target theorem both directly and as a named theorem T1. The file contains TLAPS proofs, including a one-step proof using Z3 and a more explicit stepwise proof by case distinction on whether x is even or odd.

This module models an abstract two-peer TCP finite state machine based on RFC 9293, focusing on connection-state transitions rather than low-level protocol details such as sequence numbers. It represents per-peer TCP control block existence, per-peer connection state, and in-flight network messages as sequences, and models user-triggered actions, protocol-driven state transitions, and reset behavior. The specification checks a state invariant about agreement on the ESTABLISHED state when no messages are in flight, and a liveness property that a peer in SYN-SENT eventually reaches ESTABLISHED, LISTEN, or CLOSED. The design explicitly includes RFC note-inspired transitions such as the FIN-WAIT-1 to TIME-WAIT shortcut and a reset action applicable broadly across states, and it adds weak fairness both for system steps and for a specific user close action to avoid getting stuck in SYN-SENT.

This module defines a recursive bitwise AND operation over integers and introduces an infix operator `&` as a wrapper around that recursive definition. The implementation is intended to be used with a Java operator override in TLC, as explained by the comments, and the comments also document the expected TLC behavior when the override is present or missing. The specification is not a transition-system model with variables or temporal properties; instead, it provides a mathematical/operator-level definition of bitwise conjunction using arithmetic decomposition by powers of two.

This specification models the Tower of Hanoi puzzle using three towers represented as sequences of natural numbers, where each number denotes a disk size. The initial contents of the three towers are provided by the constants A, B, and C, and the state variable towers stores the current configuration as a 3-tuple of sequences. The spec defines when a move is legal, how a move updates the towers, and a Next action that nondeterministically chooses a legal move. It also includes state invariants checking that the tower structure remains well-typed, that no new disk values are introduced, that the total number of disks remains constant, and a predicate NotSolved describing the negation of the solved configuration.

This specification models the Towers of Hanoi puzzle with a parameterized number of disks D and towers N. Towers are encoded as natural numbers whose bit patterns represent which power-of-two disk values are present on each tower, and the actions move a smallest available disk from one tower to another when the destination permits it. The spec defines an initial state, a next-state relation over legal moves, a safety-style invariant about preservation of the total disk sum, a type condition over tower values, and a temporal specification Spec asserting Init /\ [][Next]_vars; it also defines NotSolved so TLC can search for a counterexample trace reaching the solved configuration.

This module provides a TLAPS proof for the TCommit protocol, specifically for the theorem that TCSpec implies that always (TCTypeOK and TCConsistent) hold. The proof is structured hierarchically and refers to definitions and operators from the TCommit module, as well as using the TLAPS proof system. The proof demonstrates that the invariant Inv (which is TCTypeOK and TCConsistent) is preserved by the protocol's initialization and next-state actions, and that the temporal property holds globally.

This module contains TLAPS proofs about a two-phase commit specification imported from the TwoPhase module. It proves that the temporal specification TPSpec implies the type correctness invariant TPTypeOK and also implies the safety property TC!TCConsistent, which states that no resource managers can end in conflicting committed and aborted decisions. To prove consistency, the module defines a strengthened inductive invariant Inv that tracks transaction manager state, prepared messages, decision messages on the wire, and the relationship between local RM states and messages, then proves the invariant is inductive and implies the target consistency theorem.

This specification models a simple bounded FIFO queue of messages. The system starts with an empty sequence, allows sending a message from a fixed message range when the queue length is below a fixed size bound, and allows receiving by removing the head element when the queue is non-empty. The file is designed to stress TLC under anomalous conditions by generating a large state space, and it also states and checks a safety property that every element currently stored in the queue belongs to the allowed Messages set.

This specification models a simple message-shuffling system with four constant message values M0 through M3. The system maintains a set of messages on the left, a set on the right, an iteration counter, and a send count; a Send step moves one message from left to right and increments count, while an Iteration step is enabled when left is empty and moves all right-side messages back to left while incrementing the iteration number. The temporal specification asserts initialization followed by arbitrary Next steps, and the file also defines an invariant stating that the union of left and right always equals the full Messages set, together with a temporal property [] Inv. The design also includes symmetry-related helper definitions using Permutations(Messages), a fixed iteration definition, and a view tuple.

This module models heaps, objects, and promise-like objects in an object-capability style setting, including resolved and unresolved promises and actions that resolve or garbage-collect them. It defines the shape of objects, heaps, eventuals, promises, and heap well-formedness conditions such as absence of dangling pointers and acyclicity of promise chains, and it assumes semantic properties of an abstract method evaluator Eval. The file contains state-level structure definitions and three heap-updating actions for resolving when-promises, resolving non-when-promises, and garbage collecting resolved promises, but it does not define a full temporal specification or liveness/fairness properties.

This module defines and reasons about color predicates over a finite set of states. A color predicate is represented as a record with a type field indicating either "every" or "some" and a set field containing a subset of State; satisfaction means either all states in a given state set belong to the predicate set or at least one does, depending on the type. The module proves two theorems: one characterizing satisfaction over unions of state sets, and another showing how to compute satisfaction using bit-vector encodings of state sets based on a finite enumeration of State.

This module specifies the set of possible proof-obligation states for a proof management or proof-coloring system used by the TLA+ Toolbox. It models prover status information from a constant sequence of sequences of strings, defines the space of obligation states including dummy states like "missing" and "omitted" as well as ordinary proof states, and assigns each obligation state a unique consecutive number. The specification also proves that this numbering is well-formed and injective over the set of obligation states, and then instantiates another module to use this state space and its enumeration for color predicates.

This module models the structure and well-formedness of parenthesis expressions using tokens. It defines a record type Token with a type field (which can be 'left', 'right', or 'other') and an id field. The recursive operator ParenDepth computes the nesting depth of parentheses in a sequence of tokens up to a given index, incrementing or decrementing the depth based on the token type. IsWellFormed checks that a sequence never dips below zero depth and ends at zero, ensuring balanced parentheses. ExprOfMaxLen constructs the set of all well-formed sequences of tokens up to a given length n. The module does not specify a temporal system or algorithm, but rather provides structural definitions for reasoning about parenthesis expressions.

This module specifies and checks an algorithm for removing redundant matched parentheses from a well-formed token sequence representing an expression. It defines a recursive mathematical reference function Result(seq) that repeatedly removes an inner matching parenthesis pair when that pair is immediately enclosed by another matching pair, and then gives a PlusCal algorithm together with its translated TLA+ actions to compute the same result operationally. The specification uses no fault model; instead, it verifies functional correctness by asserting at termination that the algorithm's output out equals Result(in), and it also states the temporal property that the algorithm eventually reaches the control state "Done".

This module specifies data structures and algorithms for mapping a region in a TLA+ specification to corresponding PlusCal source structure, using token regions, parentheses, and breaks to describe translation correspondence. It defines location, region, token, and TPSpec well-formedness predicates, along with helper operators such as parenthesis-depth computation and region-to-token-pair selection. The file also contains a PlusCal algorithm and its generated TLA+ translation for computing the token pair selected by an input region and then scanning the token interval to compute depth information, with a temporal specification asserting the translated algorithm and a termination property.

This module specifies Bloemen et al.'s multi-core on-the-fly strongly connected components decomposition algorithm on a directed graph whose nodes and edges are given as constants. The file contains a commented PlusCal algorithm and its generated TLA+ translation, modeling shared union-find state, per-thread search state, and a work-stealing style exploration in which multiple threads cooperatively discover and merge SCC candidates while marking sets dead when fully explored. The specification defines the operational behavior with Init, Next, and Spec, adds weak fairness for both the main thread process action and the unite procedure, asserts a termination property as an eventuality that all program counters become Done, and defines a safety/correctness condition stating that upon termination the SCC partition computed by the algorithm matches the mathematical SCC decomposition by reachability.

This module specifies a message-passing abstraction in which messages are stored in a state variable as a function from message values to delivery counts. It models delivery, loss, timeout detection, processing, and sending of requests and responses, with message loss represented by a count of -1 and processed messages represented by decrementing or clearing counts. The module provides helper predicates and actions for identifying receivable messages, clearing or ignoring timed-out or superseded messages, and sending messages to a single recipient or an ensemble, but it does not define a full temporal system specification in this file.

This specification models Dijkstra's token-based distributed termination detection algorithm (EWD840). The system consists of N nodes arranged in a ring, each of which can be active or passive and colored white or black. A token circulates among the nodes, carrying a color (white or black) and a position. The algorithm ensures that global termination is detected when all nodes are passive and the token returns to node 0 as white. The model includes actions for initiating a probe, passing the token, sending messages (which can activate other nodes and stain the sender black), and deactivating nodes. The specification verifies type correctness, safety (termination detection), and liveness (eventual detection of termination), and explores the effect of different fairness conditions. Notable design decisions include the use of a weakened fairness condition (WF_vars(System)) to avoid undesired liveness properties, and the explicit modeling of node and token colors to capture the algorithm's correctness arguments.

This specification models a simplified version of the Ghostferry data-copying algorithm that copies a source database table to a target database while concurrently streaming and applying binlog entries. The model represents the system as four processes: a table iterator that copies rows, a binlog streamer that replays source updates onto the target, an application that performs concurrent INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE-style changes on the source and appends corresponding binlog entries, and a ferry coordinator that performs cutover by making the application read-only and then stopping binlog streaming after a target position is reached. The spec checks a liveness-style termination property and a safety property asserting that once all processes are done, the source and target tables are equal; it also uses fairness assumptions for all four processes and an action constraint to bound binlog growth for model checking feasibility.

This specification models a simple system where a variable x is an array indexed by a domain Dom, which is a union of two integer ranges. The system repeatedly increments x[i] modulo K for some i in Dom, and in each step, it awaits the existence of a subset s of 1..L with cardinality L. The variable y is also present and can take values in 1..C, allowing for multiple initial states. The comments explain the state space size and the computational cost of evaluating the next-state action, emphasizing the exponential blowup due to the power set operation. The spec is designed to stress-test model checking tools like TLC, especially with respect to set and function operations.

This specification models a simplified Raft-style consensus protocol for MongoDB, focusing on server roles, term numbers, and replication or rollback of per-server oplogs. The model represents each server's state and log, allows a server to become primary by a quorum-based up-to-date check, allows leaders to append client values, and allows followers to append or roll back log entries to match another server. The specification verifies the system through an initial-state predicate and a temporal next-state specification, and it also defines helper safety predicates about committed entries never being rolled back, though those verification predicates are not included in the top-level temporal specification.

This module specifies the Paxos Commit algorithm, modeling resource managers, acceptors, and leaders using a safety-only TLA+ specification. The model simplifies communication by representing msgs as the set of all messages ever sent, not explicitly modeling message receipt, and not modeling leader selection, so any process may act as leader. It defines the protocol actions for resource managers, leaders, and acceptors, gives an initial-state predicate and next-state relation, and proves that the resulting specification preserves a type-correctness invariant and implements the transaction commit specification from module TCommit.

This module specifies the Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol for distributed transactions, focusing on the behavior of resource managers (RMs). The protocol is modeled by tracking the state of each RM, which can be 'working', 'prepared', 'committed', or 'aborted'. The specification defines the possible actions (Prepare and Decide) that RMs can take, the initial state, and the next-state relation. It asserts type correctness and consistency invariants, ensuring that no two RMs reach conflicting decisions (i.e., one aborts while another commits). The main temporal property proved is that the type correctness and consistency invariants always hold under the protocol's specification.

This module specifies Lamport's Paxos consensus algorithm in the style of "Paxos Made Simple", modeling leaders by ballot number and acceptors as separate processes. It uses a message-history style model in which the variable msgs contains all messages ever sent, rather than explicitly modeling channels, message loss, or delivery; safety is expressed over what may be received from that history. The specification defines the translated PlusCal state machine, a type invariant, predicates describing when a value is chosen, and a correctness property asserting agreement-like uniqueness of chosen values; it also includes a theorem claiming that correctness is always true, with comments noting that the theorem is actually false for the current spec and should be checked with TLC.

This module specifies a simple event-counting component with a single state variable nEvents. It models a counter that starts at zero and may be incremented by the CountEvent action when a finite maximum is being enforced; if maxEvents is -1, the specification treats that as an unlimited mode and leaves the counter unchanged to avoid introducing an infinite-state model. The file defines the initialization predicate and one action, but it does not define a full temporal specification such as Spec, nor does it include fairness conditions, proofs, or PlusCal code.

This module specifies a task lifecycle system in which a variable `tasks` stores the currently allocated tasks, and tasks progress through a fixed transition table managed by different components such as the orchestrator, allocator, scheduler, agent, and reaper. The specification defines typing constraints for `tasks`, a state update action-like operator `UpdateTasks` that replaces existing tasks according to a function while preserving task identity, and a constructor `NewTask` for creating new task records from service, slot, id, and desired state information. It also defines a transition table and asserts a consistency property `TransitionTableOK` requiring monotonic state progression and non-overlapping ownership of source states across components, with limited exceptions for reaper cleanup; the file contains an ASSUME that asks TLC to check this property.

This module defines core types and helper operators for a task orchestration model resembling SwarmKit task management. It declares abstract constants for nodes, services, task IDs, and a replica bound; defines record types and task lifecycle states; and provides helper operators for state ordering, task identity, and virtual slots. The module contains no variables, actions, temporal formulas, fairness conditions, or PlusCal algorithm.

This module specifies a lower-level worker-node implementation for SwarmKit that refines a higher-level worker specification by explicitly modelling container state in addition to task state. It models worker and environment actions such as task creation and updates, manager synchronisation, container shutdown and exit, node connectivity changes, orphaning tasks when a node stays down, and worker reboot. The spec verifies that the implementation implies the higher-level worker behavior and includes temporal properties with weak fairness on agent progress actions; it also contains a theorem explaining why proving the implementation and system properties in two stages is sufficient.

This module specifies the worker-side behavior of a task orchestration system, modeling how nodes are seen by SwarmKit as either up or down and how tasks assigned to nodes progress through lifecycle states. It defines actions for normal task progress, shutdown completion, task rejection, container exit reporting, node disconnection and reconnection, and orphaning runnable tasks on nodes that remain down. The module is focused on state-transition behavior and action decomposition, and it does not itself define a temporal specification or verification theorem in this file.

This module models a small TLC-driven benchmarking harness that runs a fixed collection of TLA+ specifications sequentially with different worker counts and classifies the outcome of each run by the external process exit code. The state records the selected run number, worker count, benchmark spec name, and an IO process record, and the main action either launches TLC through an IOUtils environment-execution primitive or observes one of several terminal outcome classes: done, safety violation, liveness violation, or other violation. The file is not a protocol or fault-tolerant algorithm specification itself; instead it is an orchestration specification for executing model-checking jobs, using TLC and IO utilities, with deadlock checking disabled in the embedded TLC config block.

This module is a TLC utility specification that collects model-checking run statistics and writes them to a CSV file. It initializes the CSV output by writing a header row if the file is empty, and it defines a postcondition that records metadata about the current run, TLC revision/configuration information, and search statistics such as diameter, generated states, distinct states, queue size, and duration. The module is not a state-transition system with variables or temporal behavior; instead, it uses assumptions and constant operator definitions to orchestrate side-effecting tool calls through TLC, IOUtils, and CSV operators.

This specification defines a very small TLA+ module with one constant and one operator. The operator Bar takes an argument y and constructs a two-element tuple containing the module constant C and the argument y. The module does not define any state variables, actions, temporal behavior, fault model, or verification properties; it is purely a structural value definition.

This specification defines a very small module with a single constant C and one top-level operator Def(a). The operator constructs a labeled tuple expression lab :: <<C, a>>, so the module appears to model a simple labeled value built from the constant C and a parameter a rather than a full transition system. There are no variables, no actions, no temporal specification, no fairness conditions, and no proof content in the file.

This module is a minimal TLA+ test specification intended to exercise tooling behavior around model-checking or parsing rather than to model a substantive distributed algorithm or protocol. The comments indicate that it is related to generating parsing errors in an MC file, including malformed expressions in a spec and multiply defined symbols in another model configuration. Syntactically, the module declares one constant and one variable, and defines a single constant operator foo equal to 1; it contains no actions, no temporal specification, no fault model, and no verification properties.

This specification defines a minimal TLA+ module containing a single state variable x and one constant-valued operator foo equal to 1. The comments indicate the file is intended to trigger TLC error behavior related to configuration files and temporal formulas containing actions, but the module itself does not define an initial predicate, next-state relation, or complete temporal specification. It therefore models no full algorithm or protocol, and instead serves as a tiny test artifact illustrating tooling behavior.

This specification is a minimal test module intended to generate errors that TLC finds when evaluating assumptions. The module declares one state variable x and one constant WhichTest, but it does not define any state-transition system, initialization predicate, next-state action, or temporal specification. Its only substantive content is an ASSUME formula that selects between two test cases based on WhichTest: one branch makes the assumption false, and the other branch causes an evaluation issue by comparing the number 2 with the string "b".

This module is a minimal test specification intended to trigger various TLC behaviors or errors, as described by the header comments. The comments mention scenarios such as evaluation errors in the initial predicate, invariants, and properties, too many states, unspecified variable values, invariant violations, and property violations. Syntactically, however, the file only declares the module, extends Naturals, and declares two variables x and y; it contains no actual initial condition, next-state relation, temporal specification, or proof content.

This specification is a small test module intended to trigger different TLC model-checking outcomes, as described in the header comments. It models a simple system with two state variables, x and y, an initial state where both are 0, and several alternative next-state relations that exercise evaluation errors, excessive state growth, and underspecified next-state assignments. The module extends Naturals and includes arithmetic and function-set constructs, but it does not define a full temporal specification such as Spec; instead, it provides several candidate actions such as Next, Next1a, Next4, and Next5 for testing tool behavior.

This specification models a very small two-variable state machine with natural-number arithmetic available from the Naturals module. The initial state sets both x and y to 0, and the single step relation leaves x unchanged while toggling y between 0 and 1 using the expression 1 - y. The file comment indicates it is intended to generate a TLC error when checking temporal properties after all reachable states have been explored, but this module itself only defines the initial predicate and next-state action and does not include an explicit temporal specification or theorem.

This specification defines a very small TLA+ module containing an operator-valued constant A and a constant b, along with a single top-level definition def == A(b). It does not model any transition system, algorithm, or fault-tolerant protocol, and it introduces no variables, actions, temporal formulas, or correctness properties. The file is essentially a minimal structural example showing application of an operator-valued constant to an argument.

This TLA+ module is a minimal example that demonstrates the use of operator-valued constants and their application. The module declares a constant operator A(_) and a constant value b, then defines an operator h as the application of A to b. There are no variables, actions, temporal properties, or proofs present in this specification. The file serves as a simple illustration of operator-valued constants and their usage in TLA+.

This module defines a small collection of top-level operators intended to exercise TLA+ syntax for operator-valued constants, tuples, labeled tuple elements, set comprehension with labels, and a LET-bound local operator inside a set comprehension. It does not model a transition system: there are no variables, no actions, no temporal specification, and no safety or liveness properties. The file is purely structural and focuses on value-level definitions that reference a single operator-valued constant A5 and construct tuples and sets.

This module is a synthetic TLA+ specification designed to test parsing of subexpression references, labels, and various proof constructs. It intentionally includes constructs that are likely to produce parsing errors, such as references to 'ILLEGAL' labels and subexpressions, as well as a wide variety of proof steps, hierarchical labels, and operator definitions. The module does not model a concrete algorithm or distributed system, but rather serves as a stress test for TLA+ parsers and tools, especially in handling edge cases in proofs, subexpression references, and label usage. There are no temporal properties or fairness conditions being verified; the focus is on syntactic coverage and parser robustness.

This specification models a reconfigurable Paxos-style consensus algorithm with acceptors, ballots, instances, and configurations. It represents acceptor votes in a three-level function `avote` and the set of learned commands in `learned`, including special reconfiguration commands that install new configurations. The file proves safety properties, especially uniqueness of the learned command per instance, by defining a strong inductive invariant, auxiliary configuration-ordering functions, stability lemmas, and a substantial TLAPS proof; there are no liveness or fairness assumptions beyond the standard safety specification `Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<avote, learned>>`.

This module, test212, is a test specification for checking Leibnizness in TLA+ operator substitution. It explores the distinction between Leibniz and non-Leibniz operators, particularly in the context of substituting operators for constants in module instantiations. The file defines several operators that either are or are not Leibniz, and then attempts both legal and illegal instantiations of another module (test212a) with these operators, to illustrate which substitutions are permitted by the TLA+ semantics. The module does not specify a distributed algorithm or system, but rather serves as a meta-level test of the TLA+ language's operator substitution rules.

This TLA+ module is a minimal stub that declares two operator-valued constants, Op and Op2, with arities 1 and 2 respectively. There are no variable declarations, operator definitions, actions, temporal properties, or system modeling present in this file. The module serves as a template or placeholder for further specification development, possibly to be instantiated or extended elsewhere.

This module defines several operators to illustrate the use of primed variables, ENABLED expressions, and tuple/set constructions in TLA+. The variable y is the only state variable, and operators demonstrate both Leibniz and non-Leibniz contexts. There are no temporal properties, fairness conditions, or proofs present. The module serves as a minimal example for operator syntax and priming in TLA+.

This module is a test specification designed to check the TLA+ parser's handling of temporal formulas in non-temporal contexts and the instantiation of declared constants with temporal formulas. It contains variable declarations, instance substitutions, and several theorems with hierarchical proofs, some of which intentionally include errors to test error detection. The comments clarify that the file is for parsing only and is expected to produce errors, not to model a real algorithm or system.

This module is a minimal TLA+ specification intended primarily to illustrate the use of constants, assumptions, and a trivial theorem. It declares two constants, C and D, and assumes that C is the empty set. The theorem asserts that under the assumption D, TRUE holds, which is a tautology. There are no variables, actions, temporal properties, or algorithmic content in this specification.

This TLA+ module is a test case designed to check the syntactic restrictions on the USE and HIDE proof commands, specifically that they cannot take arbitrary expressions as facts. The file contains two theorems: one that defines a tuple and another that uses ASSUME/PROVE to demonstrate proof steps, including deliberate errors. The comments clarify the intent to test error conditions, and the module does not specify an algorithm or system but rather focuses on proof language syntax.

This module is a test specification designed to check the syntactic and semantic constraints on the use of temporal operators in TLA+. The comments and operator definitions illustrate which uses of primed variables and temporal operators are permitted and which are considered errors. The module does not model a real algorithm or system, but rather serves as a suite of test cases for the TLA+ parser or semantic checker, especially regarding the correct placement and usage of primed variables, temporal formulas, and quantification. No fault model or liveness/safety property is being verified; the focus is on language-level correctness and error detection.

This module, 'test51a', is a test specification to check the definability of certain operator aliases in TLA+. It defines several infix operators (such as =<, >=, \circ, \oplus, \ominus, \otimes, \oslash, \odot) as syntactic aliases for set enumeration of their two arguments. There are no variables, constants, temporal properties, or algorithmic content; the module is purely structural and intended for testing operator definitions.

This module defines a single operator that constructs a set containing two elements, a and b, using the syntax 'a <= b'. There are no comments or documentation in the file, and no temporal properties, variables, or constants are defined. The module appears to serve as a minimal example or test of operator definition and set enumeration in TLA+.

This specification models a simple system with a single variable x that cycles through the values 0 to 4. The initial state sets x to 0, and in each step, x is incremented by 1 modulo 5. The temporal property asserts that this incrementing behavior holds globally. The specification is intended as a test for parametrized INSTANCE, but no such instance is present in this file.

This module defines an abstract syntax tree encoded as TLA+ data for a uniprocess PlusCal-style algorithm named Euclid. The AST describes declarations for initial values u_ini and v_ini chosen from 1..MaxNum, variables u and v initialized from them, and a loop that repeatedly updates the variables using a conditional swap and subtraction pattern, followed by an assertion that v equals GCD(u_ini, v_ini). The file does not define an executable transition-system specification, temporal behavior, or fault model; instead it represents program structure as records, tuples, strings, and sequences inside TLA+ values.

This module, Pcal, specifies the translation from the abstract syntax tree (AST) of a +CAL algorithm to its TLA+ description. It provides a detailed grammar for the AST of a +CAL algorithm and defines an operator, Translation, that produces a TLA+ specification from a given AST and fairness option. The module includes a complete state machine for checking the well-formedness of the AST, as well as the translation logic for generating TLA+ code, including handling of variables, procedures, processes, and control flow constructs. The specification is executable by TLC and is intended as a partial specification for a +CAL-to-TLA+ translator, with extensive comments on known limitations, error handling, and formatting issues. It does not cover macro expansion, name collision resolution, or output formatting, and assumes all labels and variable names are distinct.

This module defines the mathematical structure and operations for bags (multisets), where a bag is a set that can contain multiple copies of the same element, with each element's multiplicity being a positive integer. The bag is represented as a function from its domain to the positive integers, and the module provides operators for bag membership, union, difference, subset, subbag enumeration, mapping, and cardinality. The specification is purely functional and declarative, with no temporal or action-based properties, and is intended for use as a standard mathematical library; most operators are overridden by TLC for model checking, except for SubBag, which is defined in a way that TLC can evaluate. The design is focused on mathematical correctness and TLC compatibility, with careful attention to finite support and computability.

This module, FiniteSets, provides definitions for two standard operators: IsFiniteSet and Cardinality. IsFiniteSet determines whether a set S is finite by checking if there exists a finite sequence containing all its elements. Cardinality computes the size of a finite set S recursively, using a LET-bound helper operator CS that counts elements by removing them one by one. The module is intended for use with TLC, which overrides these definitions in Java for efficiency, but the TLA+ definitions are mathematically precise and suitable for proof. The module imports Naturals and Sequences locally, so their definitions are not exported.

This module provides dummy definitions for the operators that are defined by the real Integers module in TLA+. It is intended as a placeholder, with the expectation that tools such as TLC will override these definitions with their own implementations. The module defines the set Int as the empty set and provides a definition for the prefix minus operator, delegating subtraction to the Naturals module. No temporal properties or algorithmic behaviors are specified.

This module defines helper operators for converting TLA+ values into JSON-like string representations and for modeling JSON serialization and deserialization interfaces. It recursively builds JSON object strings from functions or records over a finite domain, JSON array strings from sequence-like or finite-set values, and chooses between object and array formatting based on simple structural tests. The file does not model a transition system or fault-tolerant algorithm; instead, it provides pure value-level operators, including stubbed serialization operators that return TRUE and nondeterministic deserialization operators defined with CHOOSE.

This module is a dummy replacement for the standard Naturals module. Its comments explain that the operators are placeholders expected to be overridden by tools such as TLC, and that the real semantics are provided elsewhere. The file defines arithmetic, comparison, and range operators with trivial bodies so that tools can recognize and replace them; it does not model a transition system, uses no variables, and states no temporal properties.

This module defines operators for choosing pseudo-random subsets of a set, primarily for inductive invariance checking where the operators appear only in the initial predicate. The comments explain TLC-specific behavior: in breadth-first search, pseudo-random choices for a particular state are determined by the first state of the step so runs are reproducible enough to generate error traces, while in simulation mode the choices are independent of the state. The module defines a random k-element subset operator, a random set of subsets operator constrained by cardinality, and a testing operator that returns a function on 1..5 whose values are the cardinality of repeated executions of the random set-of-subsets operator. Except for TestRandomSetOfSubsets, the definitions are overridden by TLC's Java implementation.

This module defines real-time specification helpers for TLA+ by introducing a real-valued clock variable `now` and two top-level operators, `RTBound` and `RTnow`. `RTBound(A, v, D, E)` expresses that an action `A` over state tuple `v` must occur within a maximum elapsed time `E` and not before a minimum elapsed time `D`, using an existentially quantified timer variable `t` whose evolution is defined by a nested action. `RTnow(v)` constrains `now` to increase over the reals with weak fairness, providing the real-time clock assumptions needed by bounded-time specifications; the module comments explicitly note that this style of specification cannot be handled by TLC.

This module provides dummy definitions for operators that would be defined in a true Reals module, intended for use in TLA+ specifications that mention real numbers. It is not a real implementation: the operators here are placeholders, and any tool that supports real numbers is expected to provide its own correct implementation. The module defines a set Real (as the string "Reals"), a division operator a / b using CHOOSE, and an Infinity value as a CHOOSE of an element not in Real and greater than all elements of Real. The comments clarify that TLC does not support real numbers and will error if these operators are evaluated. The module extends Integers, but does not inherit any of its definitions directly.

This module defines standard operators for manipulating finite sequences in TLA+. A sequence of length n is represented as a function with domain 1..n, aligning with TLA+'s definition of tuples. The module provides constructors for sequences, length calculation, concatenation, appending elements, extracting the head and tail, subsequence extraction, and selection of elements based on a predicate. All operators are overridden by TLC for execution, but the definitions here serve as the mathematical basis for reasoning and proof. The module does not introduce any temporal properties or fault models, and is intended as a foundational library for use in other specifications.

This module defines auxiliary TLC and TLCExt operators for assertion checking, error handling, model-value creation, deferred evaluation, caching, debugging, and experimental trace/counterexample access. It is a utility module with only operator definitions and no constants, variables, actions over primed state variables, temporal specification, or PlusCal algorithm.

This module is the standard TLC support module used by the TLC model checker. It defines TLC-specific helper operators for printing, assertions, timing, stateful instrumentation via TLCGet and TLCSet, finite-function operators such as :> and @@, permutations, sequence sorting, random element selection, string conversion, and forced evaluation with TLCEval. The file contains explanatory comments about TLC's evaluation strategy, randomization behavior, and worker-thread behavior, but it does not define a state-machine specification with variables, next-state actions, fairness, or temporal properties.

This module defines helper operators for Toolbox trace exploration rather than a full transition-system specification. It models an abstract trace as a chosen function from positive natural numbers to strings, derives its length from the function domain, and computes a current trace position based on the TLC tool state via TLCGet("level"). The comments explain that _TEPosition is intended for use in TLC alias expressions and is written to account for Toolbox-specific trace-exploration behavior; there are no state variables, actions, temporal properties, fairness conditions, or proofs.

This module defines a helper operator that renders a counterexample trace as a GraphViz dot graph and writes it to a file. It inspects the TLC counterexample structure, conditionally skips output when there is no state information or when a console flag is present and set to FALSE, and otherwise constructs node and edge sets from the counterexample states and actions. The module is a utility module and does not define variables, actions, or temporal properties.

This module defines helper operators for exporting TLC counterexample traces to JSON and replaying a previously dumped JSON trace. It serializes a counterexample, reconstructs the set of variable names appearing in the trace, detects the lasso target for liveness counterexamples by finding the unique back or stuttering edge in the action graph, and defines a replay constraint that checks the current TLC state against the stored trace level by level. It also defines a replay view that includes the current level to avoid state collapsing and maps the level beyond the finite dump back to the lasso target so liveness cycles can be replayed correctly. The design relies on JSON arrays to represent serialized sets and explicitly notes assumptions about ordering and variable-subset replay compatibility.

This module defines helper operators for tracking and aggregating named occurrences of boolean conditions, apparently for instrumentation or analysis rather than for a complete state-machine specification. It uses TLC and auxiliary runtime operators to store per-name counters, merge them across workers, and check whether a named condition has been observed. The file contains only helper definitions and state-level/value-level operators, with no declared constants or variables, no transition relation, no temporal specification, and no fault model or correctness property being verified in this module itself.

This module builds and optionally writes out a TLA+ counterexample artifact to a file. It derives a module text string from the configured counterexample file name and the value of a `CounterExample` object, then conditionally serializes that generated text depending on whether the counterexample has any state and whether console output is enabled. The specification is a utility-style module rather than a transition-system model: it defines helper operators over values, uses LET-bound names, record and tuple expressions, string concatenation, and an IF-THEN-ELSE condition, but it does not declare state variables, actions, temporal behaviors, or fault-tolerance properties.

This module constructs and optionally writes out a TLA+ action-trace module representing the current TLC counterexample trace. It is a utility-oriented specification that uses TLC-provided data such as CounterExample.action, folds over the recorded actions to synthesize EXTENDS declarations and a disjunctive _next operator, and then serializes the generated text to a file. The design is centered on trace extraction and pretty-printing rather than state-transition modeling: it defines helper operators for string assembly, checks whether a counterexample exists and whether console output is enabled, and if so writes a textual module whose action constraint follows the TLC level.

This module builds and writes out a TLA+ trace module from a TLC counterexample. It computes the set of state variable names appearing in the counterexample, constructs textual conjuncts for initial and next-state relations, and assembles a generated module containing Trace, _init, _next, _terminating, and _spec. The spec is focused on trace serialization and reporting rather than verifying an algorithm directly; it also includes a guard that suppresses output when there is no counterexample state or when console output is disabled in the CounterExample record.

This module defines a small helper specification for emitting a TLC counterexample trace to a plain text TLA+ module file. It constructs a textual module containing a LOCAL INSTANCE TLC declaration and a Trace definition derived from CounterExample, then conditionally serializes that text to the file named by the constant _TLCTraceFile. The logic checks whether CounterExample.state is empty or whether console output is disabled in the CounterExample record, and otherwise requires successful serialization and prints a confirmation message; it is a utility module rather than a protocol or distributed algorithm specification.

This module provides helper operators for TLC trace serialization and replay rather than specifying a distributed algorithm. It serializes TLC counterexample traces to a file, deserializes them, constrains replayed states to match a recorded trace, and defines a view that preserves liveness lassos by mapping levels beyond the dumped prefix to the lasso target. The design relies on Java module overrides for serialization, deserialization, and state access, and it includes logic to support replay when only a subset of variables is shared between the original trace and the current specification.

This specification models an open-addressing fingerprint set with bounded probing, concurrent writer processes, and an eviction procedure that moves fingerprints from the in-memory hash table to external storage when the table is full. The PlusCal algorithm describes concurrent insertion threads, an eviction phase that sorts table contents and flushes selected entries to an external sorted sequence, and uses auxiliary variables such as history to state correctness properties. The file checks safety-style invariants about containment, duplicates, sortedness, and consistency between table and external storage, and it also specifies liveness properties such as termination and eventual completion under weak fairness for writer and eviction actions.
