desc_declarative_claude:
The module models a rolling deployment strategy for a three-server system ("s1", "s2", "s3") sitting behind a load balancer. The constant `UPDATING` represents an intermediate version state during a server upgrade.

The variables track the set of active servers in `load_balancer`, per-server boolean flags `update_flag` indicating whether a server should begin updating, and per-server `updated` values recording each server's current version state (FALSE for old, UPDATING for in-progress, TRUE for completed).

The `start_update` process orchestrates the rolling deployment in three phases: first it removes "s1" from the load balancer and triggers updates on "s2" and "s3"; then, once those servers have finished updating, it swaps the load balancer to the newly updated servers and enables "s1" to update; finally, once "s1" finishes, it is added back to the load balancer. Each `update_server` process waits for its flag, transitions through the `UPDATING` intermediate state, and then completes. All processes carry weak fairness conditions, ensuring progress is eventually made.

Two invariants are defined: `SameVersion` requires that all servers currently in the load balancer share the same version state, and `ZeroDowntime` requires that at least one server in the load balancer is not in the `UPDATING` state at any time. The spec also includes a `Termination` liveness property asserting that all processes eventually finish.
desc_intent: Specify a rolling deployment system for a cluster of three servers behind a load balancer. The deployment coordinator upgrades servers in two phases to avoid downtime: first it removes one server from the load balancer and updates it, then once the remaining servers are updated it switches the load balancer to the newly updated servers and completes the update on the original server. Each server, when signaled, transitions through an intermediate "updating" state before finishing with the new version. The system must guarantee two correctness properties throughout the deployment: zero downtime, meaning the load balancer always contains at least one server that is not currently mid-update, and same version, meaning all servers currently behind the load balancer are always running the same version of the software as each other. The specification should also guarantee termination, meaning the deployment process always eventually completes with all servers updated.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a bounded buffer shared by a nonempty set of producer processes and a nonempty set of consumer processes. The state consists of a sequence-valued buffer together with sets of currently waiting producers and waiting consumers, and the main actions describe how a producer-like step or consumer-like step either waits when the buffer is full or empty, respectively, or updates the buffer and possibly wakes a waiting process. The spec assumes producers and consumers are disjoint and that the buffer capacity is at least one, defines an initial empty state, and specifies behaviors with the temporal formula `Init /\ [][Next]_vars`. It also defines an invariant asserting that not all producers and all consumers are simultaneously waiting.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module models a classic bounded-buffer (producer-consumer) concurrency problem with multiple producers and multiple consumers sharing a fixed-capacity buffer and explicit wait sets.

Three CONSTANTS parameterize the model: `Producers` and `Consumers` are disjoint, non-empty sets of process identifiers, and `BufCapacity` is a positive natural number giving the buffer's maximum size. The three VARIABLES are `buffer` (a sequence holding items up to capacity), `waitP` (the set of producers currently blocked), and `waitC` (the set of consumers currently blocked). In the model-checking configuration, two producers `{p1, p2}`, two consumers `{c1, c2}`, and a buffer capacity of 1 are used.

The `p(self)` action represents a producer step: if the producer is not already waiting and the buffer is full, it adds itself to a wait set; otherwise it appends itself to the buffer and optionally wakes one waiting consumer. The `c(self)` action mirrors this for consumers: if the buffer is empty the consumer waits; otherwise it removes the head of the buffer and optionally wakes one waiting producer. The `Next` relation is the disjunction of all producer and consumer steps. The temporal specification `Spec` is safety-only (`Init /\ [][Next]_vars`), with no fairness constraints. The sole checked property is the invariant `Inv`, asserting that it is never the case that all producers and all consumers are simultaneously blocked — a deadlock freedom condition.
desc_intent: Write a TLA+ specification for a classic bounded producer-consumer buffer system with multiple concurrent producers and consumers. There is a fixed-capacity shared buffer, a set of producer processes that append items to the buffer, and a set of consumer processes that remove items from the buffer. Producers that attempt to add to a full buffer are suspended in a waiting set, and consumers that attempt to remove from an empty buffer are similarly suspended. When a producer successfully adds an item it may wake a waiting consumer, and when a consumer successfully removes an item it may wake a waiting producer. The sets of producers and consumers must be disjoint and non-empty, and the buffer capacity must be at least one. The key safety property to verify is that the system never reaches a state of complete deadlock in which every producer is waiting and every consumer is simultaneously waiting — that is, it is always the case that not all producers and all consumers are blocked at the same time.

This module is a parser and instantiation test for TLA+ named definitions, labels, and theorem references imported from an instantiated module rather than a behavioral system specification. It exercises many forms of INSTANCE usage, including parameterized instances, local instances, and explicit WITH substitutions, and then asserts numerous assumptions about instantiated theorem labels, operators, tuple components, and nested label selection syntax. The file contains no variables, no transition actions, no temporal specification, and no proofs; its purpose is to validate name resolution and instantiation behavior for imported labeled expressions and theorem references.

This module is a small test specification focused on the semantics of priming in TLA+ expressions and on avoiding confusion between variables, operator applications, and LET-bound names. It defines simple helper operators and a Next action that exercises priming on direct variable references, operator calls, LET expressions, and conditional branches, using TLC's Print and Assert to check expected behavior. The specification does not model faults or a distributed algorithm; instead, it serves as a semantic regression-style test over state transitions with a trivial invariant Inv == TRUE.

This specification is a small TLC-oriented test module for fingerprinting and state representation of nested function, set, and record values. It models two variables, x and y, whose values range over functions from a singleton set to functions returning subsets; y in particular ranges over subsets of records with fields a and b. The spec defines an initial predicate, an invariant that checks equality of two structurally equivalent type expressions and triggers an assertion failure if they differ, and a Next action consisting of stuttering plus several updates to x or y, including EXCEPT-based updates to nested function entries.

This module is a test specification for bag (multiset) operators written directly in TLA+, including predicates and constructors such as IsABag, SetToBag, BagCup, BagDiff, BagUnion, SubBag, BagOfAll, BagCardinality, and CopiesIn. It models bags as functions from elements to positive natural multiplicities, defines helper recursion with CHOOSE over finite subsets, and then checks a suite of expected algebraic properties and concrete examples over small bags built from the set {"a", "b", "c"}. The spec is not a fault-tolerant protocol and contains no temporal liveness properties beyond a trivial Init/Next structure; instead, it uses TLC's Print and Assert operators inside an invariant-style predicate Inv to validate correctness of the bag definitions and TLC-handled variants such as MCSubBag.

This specification is a small test module that exercises the semantics of the TLA+ UNCHANGED construct over variables and compound expressions. It defines a state with a function variable x over the range 1..3 and a scalar variable y, and the Next action is a disjunction of test cases that check whether various expressions are correctly considered unchanged, including tuples, function elements, records, quantified expressions, CHOOSE expressions, set comprehensions, and DOMAIN expressions. The module uses TLC's Print and Assert operators to validate these cases during model checking, and the only invariant stated is the trivial invariant TRUE.

This module is a small test specification for TLC fingerprinting of structured values, especially elements of function spaces of the form [S -> [B -> C]]. It initializes four variables with nested functions, records, tuples, and sequences, then allows either stuttering or a single transition that rewrites those variables into extensionally equivalent or structurally transformed values using function constructors, tuples, IF expressions, and EXCEPT updates. The spec does not model a fault-tolerant distributed algorithm; instead it is a state-space test focused on data representation and state equality, with a comment indicating TLC should find only one state.

This module is a small test specification for LET expressions and local definitions in TLA+. It defines a single variable x, a trivial initial predicate and stuttering next-state action, and focuses primarily on checking the behavior of nested LET bindings, local operator definitions, and a helper operator FcnSubst that reconstructs a function by substituting values over its domain. The invariant-like operator Inv performs three tests using Print and Assert from TLC: aliasing an empty set through LET, defining a function over an empty domain, and applying FcnSubst to a sequence-like function to confirm it increments each element as expected.

This specification models a lazy cache system with shared memory, per-processor caches, and per-processor input and output queues. The initial state constrains memory to hold initial data values, caches to hold either the corresponding memory value or a distinguished value ND, and queues to start empty; it also prints a combinatorial estimate of the state-space size. The behavior is given by arbitrary stuttering, memory updates, cache updates, queue appends, and queue tail removals, and the file defines an invariant Inv that checks type and bounded-length properties for memory, caches, and queues using diagnostic Print calls when a conjunct fails.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module is a fingerprint/regression test for TLC that models a simplified lazy-cache system. It is not intended as a complete behavioral specification of a real protocol but rather as a state-space enumeration exercise used to validate TLC's fingerprinting and state-counting correctness.

The system has four variables: `mem`, a mapping from addresses to data values representing main memory; `c`, a per-processor cache that may hold either a data value or a distinguished "not-dirty" value `ND`; `in`, a per-processor input queue of operations (reads and writes); and `out`, a per-processor output queue of data-address pairs. The constants parameterize the address set, data set, initial data subset, the sentinel value `ND`, the number of processors, and the maximum queue lengths.

The `Init` predicate initializes memory from `InitData`, caches as restrictions of memory (each cache entry is either the memory value or `ND`), and both queues as empty. It also prints the analytically computed total number of reachable states. The `Next` relation allows any combination of: leaving everything unchanged, writing any data to any address in memory, updating any cache entry, appending to or dequeueing from either per-processor queue (subject to length bounds). The invariant `Inv` checks that all variables maintain their correct types and that queue lengths remain within bounds, printing a diagnostic message identifying which conjunct fails if any does.
desc_intent:
Write a TLA+ specification that serves as a fingerprint test for a lazy cache system. The model has a shared memory mapping addresses to data values, a per-processor cache that may hold either a data value or a "not dirty" marker for each address, and per-processor input and output queues of bounded length. Input queue entries are either read or write operations (addressed data, with writes distinguished by a marker), and output queue entries are address-data pairs. The system should print the total number of distinct states at initialization so that TLC's fingerprint count can be verified against a known baseline.

The safety invariant to check is that memory always maps addresses to valid data values, each processor's cache maps addresses to data values or the no-data marker, each processor's input queue contains only valid operations and does not exceed the maximum input length, and each processor's output queue contains only address-data pairs and does not exceed the maximum output length. The specification need not enforce deep behavioral correctness beyond these type constraints, but must faithfully enumerate all relevant state transitions so the state-space size matches the analytically computed count printed at startup.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module is a small test specification that exercises basic TLA+ set, sequence, range, quantifier, conditional, and TLC printing constructs. It models a single-variable system with variable x initialized to 2, checks a collection of simple mathematical identities and existential properties in Init, and then allows only stuttering steps via Next. The design is intentionally lightweight and uses TLC's Print operator to report progress of the tests; it defines an invariant Inv == TRUE and does not include any nontrivial temporal liveness or fairness properties.

This module is a small test specification that checks proper evaluation of primed variables inside an action. It models a single-variable state machine where the initial state sets x to 2, and the only step Next constrains the next-state value x' to 2 while also asserting several expressions over x' involving arithmetic, ranges, set comprehension, filtered set comprehension, and existential quantification. The specification uses TLC's Print operator to mark progress through these checks, and it defines a trivial invariant Inv == TRUE rather than a full temporal Spec.

This module tests the equality of various representations of functions in TLA+. It defines several functions using different syntactic forms, including functions by domain, functions over tuples, and nested function constructors. The module also includes invariants that use IF-THEN-ELSE expressions to assert the correctness of function equality, and uses TLC's Assert and Print operators to report test results. The fault model is not relevant here, as this is a test harness for function representation rather than a distributed algorithm. The temporal specification is minimal, with a trivial state variable and a stuttering Next action.

This module is a small test specification that checks replacement and overriding behavior for several operator names and infix operators. It models a trivial one-variable system where the only variable x is initialized to 1 and never changes, while the Init predicate performs a sequence of assertions using IF expressions and TLC's Print and Assert operators. The specification tests operator-valued constants such as P, _++_, Plus, and PLen, along with overridden meanings for Seq and \o, and includes a LET-defined local infix operator \prec; it does not include temporal liveness properties, fairness, faults, or proofs.

This module specifies a very small state machine with two variables, x and y. The initial state sets both variables to 1 and emits a diagnostic Print message; the next-state relation either assigns x' nondeterministically from the set {1, 2, 3} while keeping y' equal to 1 and printing the generated state, or stutters by leaving both variables unchanged. The specification includes a trivial invariant Inv == TRUE and uses TLC-related printing for observation rather than for functional behavior; there is no fault model, no fairness condition, and no explicit temporal specification operator such as Spec.
desc_declarative_claude: This is a TLA+ model-checking test module designed to verify TLC's state-generation behavior and print diagnostics. It declares two variables, `x` and `y`, initialized to `1` each, with a startup message printed during initialization. The `Next` relation offers two alternatives: either `x'` is chosen nondeterministically from the set `{1, 2, 3}` while `y'` is fixed at `1` (printing a diagnostic tuple showing the newly generated state), or both variables remain unchanged via `UNCHANGED`. The invariant `Inv` is trivially `TRUE`, meaning no real safety property is enforced. The module's primary purpose is to exercise TLC's ability to enumerate distinct successor states: because `x` can take three values and `y` is always `1`, the `Next` action produces exactly three distinct states from the initial state, which matches the message printed during `Init`. The `UNCHANGED` alternative ensures the spec is non-stuttering-free and allows TLC to process the model without requiring progress. Overall, this module is a behavioral test wrapper for TLC rather than a specification of a real system or algorithm.
desc_intent: Write a small TLA+ module that demonstrates TLC's state generation and Print-based diagnostic output. The system starts with two variables both initialized to 1, and in each step either leaves both variables unchanged or nondeterministically assigns the first variable a value from the set {1, 2, 3} while keeping the second variable fixed at 1. Each transition should print diagnostic messages so that a user running TLC can observe exactly which states are being generated. The expected observable behavior is that TLC explores exactly 3 distinct reachable states (corresponding to the three possible values of the first variable). The only invariant required is the trivially true condition, meaning the specification is purely a demonstration of how TLC enumerates states and reports them via print statements rather than a model of any real system with meaningful correctness properties.
desc_perturbed: This module specifies a very small state machine with two variables, x and y. The initial state sets both variables to 1 and emits a diagnostic Print message; the next-state relation either assigns x' nondeterministically from the set {1, 2, 3} while keeping y' equal to 1 and printing the generated state, or stutters by leaving both variables unchanged. The specification includes a trivial invariant Cdy == TRUE and uses TLC-related printing for observation rather than for functional behavior; there is no fault model, no fairness condition, and no explicit temporal specification operator such as Spec.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification is a small test module for TLA+ action-subscript operators, specifically the box-style form [A]_e and the angle-bracket form <<A>>_e. It defines two variables x and y, initializes both to 1, and then uses a Next action with several branches that check whether stuttering and non-stuttering action formulas over different state expressions evaluate as expected. The module uses TLC-specific operators Print and Assert to validate these semantic cases rather than modeling a fault-tolerant protocol or distributed algorithm, and it includes a trivial invariant Inv == TRUE.

This specification is a small state-space test that models a single variable x ranging over the set of all functions from 1..6 to 1..7. The initial predicate prints a status message using TLC's Print operator and then chooses any such function as the initial value of x, while the next-state relation allows only stuttering by leaving x unchanged. It defines a trivial invariant TRUE and appears intended to measure or demonstrate exploration of a large finite set of function states rather than verify a nontrivial safety or liveness property.

This specification is a small test module for TLC model values. It declares three constants a, b, and c, one variable x, initializes x to 1, and defines only stuttering behavior by leaving x unchanged in Next. The main property-like operator Inv checks that the model value a is not treated as a string, not equal to the concrete set {1, 2}, not a member of a numeric set comprehension, and not a member of the explicitly enumerated set {b, c}; each check uses Assert on failure and Print on success.

This module is a small regression-style specification that tests the standard TLA+ Sequences module and selected TLC operators. It models a trivial one-variable system where the state variable x is initialized to 0 and never changes, while the operator Inv contains a conjunction of sequence-related checks such as membership in Seq(Nat), concatenation with \o, Len, Append, Head, Tail, SubSeq, and SelectSeq. The design uses TLC's Print and Assert operators to report success or failure of each test case, and it includes local LET-defined predicate operators for SelectSeq tests; there are no temporal properties, fairness conditions, faults, or proofs.

This module is a regression-style test specification for the standard TLA+ Bags module. It defines two bags derived from small string sets and then checks a sequence of bag-related properties such as membership, conversion to sets, empty-bag behavior, bag addition and subtraction, bag union, subbag ordering, mapping with BagOfAll, and bag cardinality/copy counts. The spec uses a single variable x with a trivial stuttering next-state relation, and the main interesting behavior is in the state predicate Inv, which uses IF/THEN/ELSE together with TLC's Print and Assert to validate expected results; comments note that tests involving SubBag are disabled because TLC did not implement that operator.

This module is a small test specification for the standard FiniteSets module. It declares a single variable x, initializes it to 0, and defines a stuttering Next action that keeps x unchanged. The main operator Inv is a state-level conjunction of four IF-THEN-ELSE checks that test IsFiniteSet and Cardinality on the empty set and on the finite set {"a", "b"}, using TLC's Print and Assert operators to report success or failure.

This specification is a small test module that checks use of EXTENDS with a user-defined module and TLC. It models a one-variable system where the initial condition is given by the imported operator MInit applied to x, and the next-state action sets x' equal to c. It also defines an invariant-style state predicate Inv that uses an IF expression and TLC's Print operator to report whether the current value of x equals c.

This specification is a small test module that exercises priming behavior and operator arguments in TLA+. It defines two state variables, x and y, initializes x as a function over the set {1,2}, and then defines a Next action with two non-stuttering branches plus a stuttering branch. The purpose of the test is to distinguish how priming behaves when action operators are called with variables as arguments, specifically comparing an operator that uses d' inside an EXCEPT update with one that uses d unprimed, and checking the resulting next-state value with TLC Print and Assert calls.

This module is a small test specification for TLA+ function application and related value expressions. It checks, through the invariant Inv, that function constructors and record-style application behave as expected, using TLC operators Assert and Print to report success or failure of individual tests. The active part of the file models a trivial one-variable system where x is fixed at 1, with Type constraining the state, Init initializing x, and Next stuttering; many additional test cases are present but commented out and therefore not extracted as active syntax.

This module is a small test specification for the standard Naturals module, using TLC helper operators to report success or failure of arithmetic checks. It models a trivial one-variable system in which x is initialized to 0 and never changes, while the main invariant Inv consists of a conjunction of arithmetic and comparison tests over exponentiation, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulo, ordering, set membership in Nat, and range expressions. The design intentionally puts all substantive behavior in a state predicate rather than in actions or temporal properties, and it uses Print and Assert from TLC to validate expected results.

This module is a small regression-style TLA+ specification that tests the semantics of the standard Integers module together with TLC utility operators. It declares a single variable x, initializes it to 0, and uses a stuttering Next action so the behavior itself is trivial. The main content is the state predicate Inv, which contains a conjunction of integer arithmetic, exponentiation, division, modulo, comparison, membership in Int, and range-expression checks; each test prints a success message or raises an assertion failure through TLC if the expected integer behavior does not hold.

This module is a small test specification for TLA+ operator arguments. It checks that user-defined operators and built-in infix operators can be passed as arguments to higher-order operators, using helper definitions like FooBar and Foo and validating the results through TLC's Print and Assert operators. The state space itself is trivial, with a single variable x, an initialization x = 1, a stuttering Next action x' = x, and a state predicate Inv that contains several IF-THEN-ELSE checks for expected arithmetic results.

This specification is a small test module for TLC operators and library functionality rather than a distributed algorithm. It defines a fold-like operator FApply over finite-domain functions, a BoundedSeq operator that constructs all sequences over a set up to a given length, simple arithmetic helpers Plus and Times, and an invariant Inv that checks a collection of expected TLC evaluation results using Print and Assert. The model uses a single variable x with a trivial stuttering Next action x' = x, and the main substantive content is the state predicate Inv containing test assertions about function application, bounded sequences, sequence lengths, and sequence sorting.

This module is a parser and precedence test for a wide variety of user-definable infix operators in TLA+. It declares a single variable x with a trivial stuttering next-state action, then defines many custom infix operators that all return a tuple <<a, b>>, and uses the operator Inv to check associativity and precedence relationships by evaluating expressions and invoking TLC's Print and Assert operators. The specification is not modeling a distributed algorithm or fault-tolerant protocol; instead, it is validating syntactic binding behavior of operators, sequence concatenation, and precedence interactions among custom operators and built-in symbols.

This module is a test specification for recursive function definitions in TLA+. It defines three recursively specified functions, f, g, and h, over small finite numeric domains and checks that they evaluate to the expected values and domains. The state space itself is trivial, with a single variable x initialized to 2 and never changed, and the main property is an invariant that uses TLC's Print and Assert operators to validate recursive computation results.

This specification models a simple request-issuing system in which processors maintain per-processor request queues and a global partial order over request identifiers. The model defines typed request and free-register values, initializes all processor queues to the empty sequence, and allows a processor to issue a request by appending a register record to its queue while extending the global request order monotonically. It checks structural properties such as a type invariant, a well-formed request ordering relation with transitivity, irreflexivity, and per-processor index order, and also includes a queue-length constraint limiting each processor queue to fewer than two elements.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module is a TLA+ test case (described as having caught a bug in an early TLC version) that models a simplified request-ordering system for a multiprocessor memory architecture.

The model has two variables: `reqQ`, a per-processor sequence of issued requests, and `reqOrder`, a binary relation over request identifiers capturing the global ordering of requests. The constant parameters are `Reg` (registers), `Adr` (addresses), `Val` (values), and `Proc` (processors). Each request identifier (`reqId`) is a record pairing a processor with an index into that processor's queue.

The sole action, `IssueRequest`, appends a new request entry (carrying a register field) to a chosen processor's queue and nondeterministically extends `reqOrder` via `UpdateReqOrder`. The updated order must be a superset of the old one, must remain a subset of the new `reqId` cross product, and must satisfy `GoodReqOrder`, which enforces transitivity, irreflexivity, and the constraint that program order (earlier indices on the same processor) is respected.

The state space is bounded by a model constraint limiting each processor's queue to fewer than two entries. The temporal specification is defined by `Init` and `Next` with no fairness conditions. The checked invariant is `TypeInvariant`, which asserts that `reqQ` maps each processor to a sequence of requests or register-tagged records, and that `reqOrder` is a subset of the appropriate cross product of request identifiers.
desc_intent: Write a TLA+ specification for a small test model of a multiprocessor request-ordering system, intended to verify correct handling of a request queue and ordering relation. Each processor maintains a sequence of pending requests, where each request carries an address, a value, and an operation type (read or write). Processors may issue new requests, appending them to their queue and updating a global partial order over request identifiers (each identified by processor and queue index). The ordering relation must remain a strict partial order — irreflexive and transitive — and must respect per-processor program order, meaning earlier-issued requests from the same processor always precede later ones. When new requests are issued, the ordering relation may grow but must never lose existing order pairs. The type invariant requires the queue map and order relation to have the appropriate types at all times. Use small finite constants (two processors, one register, one address, two values) and bound queue length to keep the state space tractable. The key correctness property to check is the type invariant.
desc_perturbed: This specification models a simple request-issuing system in which processors maintain per-processor request queues and a global partial order over request identifiers. The model defines typed request and free-register values, initializes all processor queues to the empty sequence, and allows a processor to issue a request by appending a register record to its queue while extending the global request order monotonically. It checks structural properties such as a type invariant, a well-formed request ordering relation with transitivity, irreflexivity, and per-processor index order, and also includes a queue-length constraint limiting each processor queue to fewer than two elements.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a very small integer-state transition system over a single variable x. The initial state sets x to -1, and the next-state relation decrements x by 1 unless x is already -3, in which case it stutters on x. The file appears intended to check module extension behavior, specifically EXTENDS of another module together with Integers, and it defines a trivial invariant Inv == TRUE rather than asserting a temporal correctness property.

This module is a small test specification whose purpose is to exercise user-definable infix, postfix, and prefix operators in TLA+. It defines a single variable x, an initial condition setting x to 0, and a Next action that assigns x' to the result of applying many custom operators to x and the constant 1. The spec does not define a full temporal Spec formula or verify liveness or safety properties; instead, it is structured as a parsing and definability test for operator syntax, while also extending TLC because some related operators are mentioned in comments as already defined there.

This module is a small test specification for definability of user-defined infix operators with aliases that resemble built-in TLA+ operators. It declares a single variable x, defines several infix operators such as (+), (-), (.), (/), (\X), \o, %, \leq, and \geq, and then uses them inside the Next action to confirm they can be parsed and referenced as ordinary user-defined operators. The specification does not define a temporal Spec operator or verification theorem; it is primarily a syntactic/operator-definition test over a one-variable state machine.

This module is a small parser and definability test for user-defined infix operators with alias-like symbolic names. It declares a single variable x, defines several infix operators such as (+), (-), (.), (/), (\X), \o, %, \leq, and \geq to all return their left operand, and then uses them in the Next action to test whether the syntax is accepted. The specification does not define a temporal Spec operator or any liveness or safety theorem; instead it initializes x to 0 and uses TLC's Print operator in Init while Next nondeterministically assigns x' using the custom infix operators, with comments noting parser or TLC bugs for some forms.

This specification tests the fingerprinting of sets in TLA+ by assigning various set and function values to variables and observing their behavior under TLC. The variables x, y, z, and w are assigned sets, sets of sets, records, and sets of functions, respectively. The Init operator initializes these variables with specific values, and the Next operator allows x to be updated to a set with repeated elements, while the other variables remain unchanged. The spec includes an invariant Inv that asserts the variables retain their initial values. The comments and Print statements indicate the purpose is to check that TLC recognizes only one distinct state despite syntactic differences in set representations. No fault model is present, and the properties focus on state equality and set semantics.

This module is a small regression-style TLA+ specification that tests usability of several standard-module operator aliases. It checks that bag addition and subtraction aliases from Bags, sequence concatenation aliases from Sequences, and comparison aliases from Naturals behave equivalently to their corresponding canonical operators. The spec declares a single variable x with a trivial initial predicate and stuttering next-state action, while the main interesting predicate Inv consists of a conjunction of IF-THEN-ELSE checks that call TLC's Print and Assert operators to validate the expected equalities.

This module is a parser-oriented regression test for TLA+ infix operator symbols. It defines many user-defined infix operators, passes operator symbols as arguments to higher-order operators, and checks via a single ASSUME block that parsing and operator binding behave as expected for undefined infix operators, TLC-specific operators, built-in boolean operators, and built-in set operators.

This module is a test specification for passing TLA+ prefix and postfix operators as operator arguments and for defining custom prefix and postfix operators. It checks that operators such as `[]`, `<>`, `ENABLED`, `UNCHANGED`, `SUBSET`, `UNION`, `DOMAIN`, and the prime operator can be supplied to higher-order operator definitions and used syntactically in definitions and assumptions. The spec also includes a tiny two-variable state machine over sets, defines a standard `Spec` and a derived temporal `Property`, and uses an ASSUME block with TLC `Print` calls to validate expected parsing and evaluation behavior.

This module is a small test specification for definability of custom infix operators with alias-like symbols. It defines several binary operators, including operator names that resemble built-in arithmetic or comparison syntax, and uses them in a simple next-state action over a single variable x. The specification does not define a full temporal Spec operator or temporal properties; instead it focuses on whether these operator definitions can be parsed and used in state transitions, with comments noting TLC bugs for some operator spellings.

This module is a small parser and operator-definability test for user-defined infix operators and aliases in TLA+. It defines a single variable x, initializes it to 0, and specifies a Next action that assigns x' using several custom infix operators and aliases, with comments noting parser or TLC bugs for some forms. The file does not define a full temporal specification or verify liveness or safety properties; instead it focuses on whether unusual operator spellings and symbolic aliases can be defined and then used in expressions and actions.

This specification models a very small one-variable transition system over the variable z, initialized to 0 and updated by toggling between 0 and 1 via the action Next. It instantiates another module, test55a, by substituting both instance parameters x and y with z, and then defines properties in terms of instance-exported operators such as F, G, Init, SafeSpec, and LiveSpec. The temporal specification requires the initial condition, that every step satisfies Next up to stuttering, and weak fairness of Next; it also asserts an invariant combining instance properties and exposes imported safety and liveness properties through the instance.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module `test55` is a model-checking test that verifies the behavior of `ENABLED` within an `INSTANCE` substitution context by importing definitions from the module `test55a`.

The single variable `z` ranges over natural numbers, initialized to `0`, and toggles between `0` and `1` via the `Next` action (`z' = 1 - z`). The temporal specification `Spec` combines this initialization, a stuttering-tolerant always-`Next` box formula, and weak fairness on `Next` with respect to `z`.

The module instantiates `test55a` as `I`, substituting both parameters `x` and `y` with `z`. The invariant `Invariant` asserts that `I!F` holds and `I!G` does not hold in every reachable state. The properties `InitProperty`, `SafeProperty`, and `LiveProperty` expose corresponding predicates and temporal formulas from the instantiated module under those substitutions.

The model-checking configuration runs the `Spec` specification, checks `Invariant` as a state invariant, and checks `InitProperty` as a temporal property. The module's primary purpose is to test that TLC correctly handles `ENABLED` semantics when variables are renamed through module instantiation, rather than to model a meaningful concurrent system.
desc_intent: Write a TLA+ specification that tests the semantics of ENABLED when used with module instantiation. The setup involves a single boolean-like variable that toggles between 0 and 1, with a fairness condition ensuring it keeps toggling forever. A separate module is instantiated by mapping both of that module's variables to this single variable, effectively making them aliases of each other. The correctness properties to verify include an invariant combining two conditions drawn from the instantiated module (one that must hold, one that must not hold), a property asserting that the instantiated module's initial condition holds in the initial state, and additional properties imported from the instantiated module covering both safety and liveness. The purpose is to confirm that ENABLED expressions and related temporal properties behave correctly under module instantiation with substitution, particularly when multiple formal parameters are mapped to the same concrete variable.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification is a small test module about subtle semantics of TLA+ INSTANCE with substitution. It declares a single state variable x, instantiates module test56a as I with the substitution u <- x, and defines operators to compare an instantiated action-related expression against a manually written counterpart. The behavior of the system itself is given by Init, Next, and Spec, where x starts in 1..3 and then evolves according to x' = 9-x; the temporal property Property asserts, under stuttering semantics over x, that the instantiated expression I!H equals NotIBangH in all behaviors.

This module is a small test specification that checks the parsing and meaning of binary, octal, and hexadecimal numeric literals in TLA+. It extends Naturals and contains a single unnamed ASSUME block asserting that several binary, octal, and hexadecimal notations all denote the decimal value 63. The file does not model a transition system or algorithm, has no variables or actions, and contains no temporal properties; its purpose is purely to validate numeric literal syntax across upper- and lower-case base prefixes and hexadecimal digits.

This specification models a single-variable state machine over the variable y, initialized to 0 and updated by a modular arithmetic step. The next-state action uses a LET block that binds a local value x and creates a local INSTANCE of module test59a, then assigns y' using the instantiated operator M!xplus1 in the expression (M!xplus1 - 1) % 5. The spec defines the standard temporal behavior as Init /\ [][Next]_y /\ WF_y(Next), asserts a state invariant that y remains in the range 0..4, and states a liveness property []<>(y = 4). A notable design detail is that the INSTANCE appears inside a LET expression.
desc_declarative_claude:
This is a model-checking test module that verifies the behavior of a `LET` expression containing both a local operator definition and a local `INSTANCE` of another module (`test59a`).

The module has a single variable `y`. The `Init` predicate sets `y` to `0`. The `Next` action uses a `LET` block to define a local value `x` equal to `y+1` and instantiates the module `test59a` as `M` (presumably passing `x` as a parameter substitution), then advances `y` to `(M!xplus1 - 1) mod 5`. This effectively increments `y` by one modulo 5 each step, cycling through values `0` through `4`. The `Spec` combines `Init`, the always-enabled stuttering next-state relation `[][Next]_y`, and weak fairness on `Next`, ensuring the system keeps stepping rather than stuttering forever.

The module declares an invariant `Invariant` stating that `y` always remains in the range `0..4`, and a liveness property `Liveness` asserting that `y` repeatedly reaches the value `4`. The configuration file designates `Spec` as the temporal specification and `Liveness` as the property to check. The primary purpose of this module is to test that TLA+ correctly handles `INSTANCE` appearing inside a `LET` expression.

The module specifies a multi-instance consensus problem, extending a basic single-value consensus model to an array of independent consensus slots. It is parameterized by two constants: `Values`, a non-empty set of candidate values, and `Slots`, a non-empty set of consensus instance identifiers.

The state consists of two variables: `proposed`, a set of values that have been proposed, and `chosen`, a function mapping each slot to a set of chosen values (initially empty). Two actions drive the system. `Propose` non-deterministically selects a value from `Values` that has not yet been proposed and adds it to `proposed`. `Choose` selects a slot whose `chosen` set is still empty and assigns to it a singleton set containing some already-proposed value. The temporal specification `Spec` is the standard safety spec; `LiveSpec` adds weak fairness over all transitions.

Four safety properties are stated and asserted to follow from `Spec`. `TypeOK` enforces that `chosen` maps slots to finite subsets of `Values`. `Nontriviality` requires that any chosen value was previously proposed. `Stability` requires that once a value is chosen in a slot it remains chosen forever. `Consistency` requires that each slot holds at most one chosen value. A liveness property, `Liveness`, asserts that under `LiveSpec` every slot eventually has a chosen value. The model-checking configuration instantiates the spec with two values and two slots, checks all four safety properties as invariants/properties, and verifies the liveness property.
desc_intent: Specify a multi-instance consensus system over a fixed set of named slots, each of which must independently reach consensus on a value drawn from a fixed nonempty set of values. No value may be chosen for any slot unless it was previously proposed (nontriviality). These three are the core safety properties. For liveness, under fair execution every slot must eventually have a chosen value. Assume both the set of values and the set of slots are nonempty. The specification should be checked with two values and two slots, verifying the type invariant as an invariant and all four properties — nontriviality, stability, consistency, and liveness — as temporal properties, with deadlock checking disabled.

desc_intent:

desc_declarative_claude:
The Chameneos module specifies the "Chameneos" concurrency game, in which a population of color-changing creatures (chameneoses) repeatedly meet at a shared meeting place and mutually adopt a new color determined by the complement of their two colors.

The model has two constants: `N`, the total number of meetings allowed before creatures fade, and `M`, the number of chameneoses. The three variables are `chameneoses`, a function mapping each creature's ID to its current color and personal meeting count; `meetingPlace`, recording which single creature (if any) is currently waiting; and `numMeetings`, the global count of completed meetings. Colors are drawn from `{"blue", "red", "yellow"}`, plus a special `Faded` value. The complement of two distinct colors is the third color; the complement of two identical colors is that same color.

In the `Meet` action, a non-faded chameneos either enters an empty meeting place (if the global count has not yet reached `N`), fades immediately (if `numMeetings = N` and the place is empty), or completes a meeting with the waiting creature (if the place is occupied by a different creature), in which case both creatures adopt the complement color, each increments its personal meeting count, and the global count advances. The system's next-state relation requires that at least one non-faded chameneos acts. The specification uses `Init /\ [][Next]_vars` with no fairness condition. The checked invariant `SumMet` asserts that once `numMeetings` reaches `N`, the sum of all individual meeting counts equals `2*N`.
desc_intent: Specify the Chameneos concurrency game as described in the original benchmark paper. The system involves M creatures (chameneos), each starting with one of three colors (blue, red, yellow), that repeatedly attempt to meet at a shared meeting place (mall). The mall holds at most one waiting creature at a time. When a creature arrives at an empty mall and the total meeting count has not yet reached N, it waits; when a second creature arrives, the two meet, each adopting the complement color of the pair (if colors differ, both take the third color; if identical, both keep their color), and each increments its personal meeting count. Once N total meetings have occurred, any creature arriving at the mall instead fades permanently. The system terminates when all creatures have faded. The key safety property is that once exactly N total pairwise meetings have occurred, the sum of all individual creatures' personal meeting counts equals 2*N. Type correctness must also be maintained throughout. Deadlock need not be considered a failure condition.

desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies the classic Cigarette Smokers Problem, a concurrency problem from 1971. Three ingredients (matches, paper, and tobacco in the model configuration) are shared between a dealer and smokers, where each smoker has an infinite supply of exactly one ingredient and needs the other two to roll and smoke a cigarette.

`Ingredients` is a constant set of all ingredients, and `Offers` is a constant set of subsets, each containing all ingredients except one. The variable `smokers` maps each ingredient to a record tracking whether that smoker is currently smoking, and `dealer` holds the current offer on the table (a subset from `Offers`) or an empty set when no offer is present. In the initial state, all smokers are idle and the dealer has already placed some offer. The `startSmoking` action fires when the dealer has made an offer: it sets the smoker whose missing ingredient completes the full set to smoking and clears the dealer's offer. The `stopSmoking` action fires when the dealer's table is empty: it finds the one currently smoking smoker, marks them as done, and has the dealer place a new offer. The temporal specification `Spec` is `Init` with a always-enabled `Next` step, and `FairSpec` adds weak fairness over all variables. The model checks two invariants: `TypeOK`, asserting well-typed state, and `AtMostOne`, asserting that no more than one smoker smokes at any given moment.
desc_intent: Specify the Cigarette Smokers Problem as a TLA+ model. There are three ingredients (matches, paper, tobacco) and three smokers, each of whom possesses an infinite supply of exactly one ingredient. A dealer repeatedly places two of the three ingredients on the table. The smoker who holds the missing ingredient picks up the offered pair, combines them with their own supply, and smokes; when done smoking, the dealer places a new pair on the table. The system should be parameterized by a set of ingredients and a set of offers, where each offer is a subset of ingredients of size one less than the full set. The model must capture the dealer selecting an offer, a smoker recognizing they hold the complementary ingredient and beginning to smoke, and the smoker eventually finishing and signaling the dealer to proceed. The key safety property is mutual exclusion: at most one smoker may be smoking at any given moment. This module specifies the Dining Philosophers problem for N philosophers arranged in a ring, with a semaphore-like variable sem representing fork availability and a control-state variable pc representing each philosopher's program counter. desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies the Dining Philosophers problem using the Chandy-Misra solution, implemented in PlusCal and translated to TLA+. The system models NP philosophers (instantiated as 5 in the configuration) seated in a circle, each sharing a fork with each neighbor. The single global variable `forks` is a function from fork indices to records tracking the current holder and whether the fork is clean or dirty. Each philosopher process has a local `hungry` flag. Initially, every fork is dirty and held by the lower-numbered adjacent philosopher, except fork 2 which is held by philosopher 1.

Each philosopher process runs a fair, infinite loop with three labeled steps. In the `Loop` step, if the philosopher holds a dirty left or right fork, they clean it and pass it to the neighboring philosopher; if hungry and able to eat (holding both forks, both clean), they transition to `Eat`; otherwise if not hungry, they transition to `Think`. The `Eat` step sets the philosopher's state to not-hungry and marks both held forks as dirty. The `Think` step simply sets the philosopher back to hungry. The temporal specification requires weak fairness for every philosopher process, ensuring no process is indefinitely blocked. The model checks two invariants — `TypeOK` (type correctness of all variables) and `ExclusiveAccess` (no two neighboring philosophers eat simultaneously) — and one liveness property, `NobodyStarves`, asserting that every philosopher eats infinitely often.
desc_intent: Specify the Dining Philosophers problem using the Chandy-Misra solution. There are N philosophers sitting in a circle, each needing two forks (shared with immediate neighbors) to eat. Unlike Dijkstra's original formulation, philosophers may directly hand forks to one another. Each fork has an owner and a cleanliness state: forks start dirty, and after eating a philosopher must clean a dirty fork before passing it to a requesting neighbor. Initially every fork is held dirty by the lower-numbered of its two adjacent philosophers. Each philosopher cycles between hungry and thinking states, passing dirty forks to neighbors when requested, and eating only when holding both adjacent forks in a clean state; after eating, both forks become dirty. All philosophers must be modeled as fair processes that never permanently stop. The specification must satisfy two safety invariants: type correctness of all state variables, and mutual exclusion meaning no two philosophers who share a fork may eat simultaneously. The key liveness property is that no philosopher ever starves — every philosopher must eat infinitely often, i.e., every hungry philosopher eventually gets to eat regardless of how other philosophers behave.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module models a bounded multi-producer, multi-consumer Disruptor-style ring buffer. Producers claim sequence numbers, write their claimed sequence into a shared ring buffer, and publish availability; consumers read published entries in multicast fashion so that every consumer should eventually observe every published value. The specification checks absence of producer-consumer data races via an instantiated RingBuffer module, basic typing and bounded-state constraints, and a liveness property stating that for every reader and every publishable index below the bound, eventually always: if that index is available, then the reader has that value recorded at the corresponding position in its consumption history.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies a Multi-Producer, Multi-Consumer (MPMC) Disruptor ring buffer, a high-performance concurrent data structure in which multiple writer threads publish events and multiple reader threads consume every published event (multicast semantics).

The model is parameterized by `Writers` (producer thread identifiers), `Readers` (consumer thread identifiers), `Size` (ring buffer capacity), `MaxPublished` (an upper bound on published events used to keep model checking finite), and `NULL`. Key variables track the ring buffer contents, a shared atomic counter `next_sequence` for sequence claiming, each writer's `claimed_sequence`, a per-slot `published` flag encoded as an even/odd round bit to detect availability without requiring a separate cursor, per-reader `read` cursors, per-consumer `consumed` history sequences, and a program counter `pc` for each thread with states `Access` and `Advance`.

Producer behavior proceeds in two steps: `BeginWrite` atomically claims the next sequence number (guarded so producers cannot lap consumers by a full ring cycle) and writes a value, then `EndWrite` flips the slot's published bit to signal availability. Consumer behavior similarly splits into `BeginRead`, which waits until the next sequence is published and records the read value in `consumed`, and `EndRead`, which advances the reader's cursor. The `AvailablePublishedSequence` function computes the highest contiguous published sequence visible to consumers, accounting for gaps where slower producers have not yet published. The temporal specification adds weak fairness for all consumer actions. Safety invariants check `TypeOk` and `NoDataRaces` (no concurrent reader/writer access to the same slot). The liveness property `Liveliness` asserts that every reader eventually and permanently has consumed all published values in the correct order up to `MaxPublished`.
desc_intent:
Specify a Multi-Producer, Multi-Consumer (MPMC) Disruptor ring buffer. The system has a fixed number of producer threads and consumer threads sharing a bounded ring buffer. Producers atomically claim monotonically increasing sequence numbers, write their claimed sequence number as a value into the corresponding ring buffer slot, and then publish the slot. Multiple producers may claim sequences concurrently, so a slot is only considered available to consumers once all preceding slots have also been published. Consumers operate in multicast fashion: every consumer must independently read every published event in sequence order, and a producer may not overwrite a slot until all consumers have advanced past it.

The specification must guarantee two safety properties: no data races occur on ring buffer slots (no concurrent reads and writes or concurrent writes to the same slot), and the ring buffer type invariant holds throughout execution. For liveness, the specification must guarantee that under weak fairness of consumer steps, every consumer eventually reads all published values, and the value read at each position equals the sequence number claimed by whichever producer wrote it. The model should be bounded by a maximum number of published events and a configurable ring buffer size, with the number of producers and consumers left as parameters.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module models a Single Producer, Multi Consumer Disruptor using a ring buffer. A producer publishes sequence numbers into the buffer, while multiple consumers read them, and the specification checks that all consumers read all published values in multicast style. The model uses bounded constants such as MaxPublished and Size, includes a state constraint to bound exploration, asserts type correctness and absence of data races through the instantiated ring buffer module, and states a liveness property requiring every consumer to eventually always have read each published value.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies a Single Producer, Multi-Consumer (SPMC) Disruptor, a high-performance ring-buffer-based event-passing pattern. One writer thread publishes events into a fixed-size ring buffer while multiple reader threads independently consume every published event in a multicast fashion—each consumer reads every event, not just one.

The state consists of the ring buffer itself (managed by an instantiated `RingBuffer` module), a single `published` write cursor (an integer initialized to −1), per-consumer `read` cursors, per-thread program counters (`Access` or `Advance`), and a history variable `consumed` that records the sequence of values each reader has observed. Production is split into `BeginWrite`/`EndWrite` steps: a writer may only claim the next slot once all consumers are at least one full buffer cycle behind, preventing overwrite of unread data. Consumption is likewise split into `BeginRead`/`EndRead` steps, gated on the published cursor having advanced past the reader's next sequence number. The model is bounded by the `StateConstraint` `published < MaxPublished` (set to 10 in the config), with one writer and three readers over a ring of size 4.

Weak fairness is imposed on both consumer actions to ensure readers make progress. The invariants `TypeOk` and `NoDataRaces` assert well-typed state and absence of concurrent read/write conflicts on any slot. The liveness property `Liveliness` asserts that every consumer eventually and permanently has read every published value in order, with `consumed[r][i+1] = i` confirming that the sequence number itself was stored as the slot's value.
desc_intent:
Specify a Single Producer, Multiple Consumer (SPMC) Disruptor ring buffer in TLA+. The system consists of exactly one producer thread and one or more consumer threads sharing a fixed-size circular ring buffer. The producer publishes events sequentially into the ring buffer, writing each slot exclusively before advancing its write cursor. Each consumer independently reads every published event in order, advancing its own read cursor after each access. The producer must not overwrite a slot until all consumers have advanced past it (i.e., the producer may be at most one full buffer capacity ahead of the slowest consumer).

The specification must enforce two correctness properties. First, a safety property: no data races occur, meaning the producer never writes a slot while any consumer is reading it, and no two threads access the same slot concurrently in conflicting ways. Second, a liveness property: every consumer must eventually read every published value, and the value read at each position must equal the sequence number published there (multicast semantics — all consumers receive all events). Weak fairness should be assumed for consumer actions. The model should be bounded by a maximum number of published events to make model checking feasible.

desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies a solution to the classic "Prisoners and Switches" puzzle. A warden repeatedly selects prisoners at random to enter a room with two switches (A and B), each of which must be flipped exactly once per visit. One designated prisoner, `Counter`, uses switch A to tally visits; every other prisoner flips switch A up at most twice if it is down, and otherwise toggles switch B. The counter flips switch A down whenever it is up and increments an internal count; otherwise the counter toggles switch B. When `count` reaches `2 * (Cardinality(Prisoner) - 1)`, the counter declares that all prisoners have visited, and the group is freed (`Done`).

The four variables are `switchAUp`, `switchBUp` (boolean switch states), `timesSwitched` (a function from non-counter prisoners to how many times each has raised switch A, bounded at 2), and `count` (the counter's tally, bounded at `2 * Cardinality(Prisoner) - 1`). The initial state allows the switches to start in any position. Fairness requires every prisoner's action to be weakly fair, encoding the warden's guarantee that each prisoner visits infinitely often. The safety property asserts that `Done` can only become true when every non-counter prisoner has flipped switch A at least once (guaranteeing correctness of the declaration), and the liveness property asserts that `Done` is eventually reached. An auxiliary invariant, `CountInvariant`, relates `count` to the total number of upward flips and the current state of switch A, and is used to establish the safety argument. The model is checked with four prisoners for `TypeOK`, `CountInvariant`, `Safety`, and `Liveness`.
desc_intent:
Specify a solution to the following puzzle: a warden places a group of prisoners in a situation where they must collectively determine when all of them have visited a certain room at least once. The room contains two switches, each up or down. The warden selects prisoners one at a time, in any order, and each selected prisoner must flip exactly one switch. The prisoners agree on a strategy in advance but cannot communicate afterward. At any point a prisoner may declare that everyone has visited the room; if correct they go free, if wrong they are all executed. The switches start in an arbitrary unknown position.

Model the agreed-upon counting strategy, in which one designated prisoner acts as counter and the rest are non-counters. The initial switch states are nondeterministic. Fairness must guarantee every prisoner is selected infinitely often. The specification must satisfy two properties: safety, meaning that whenever the counter declares completion every non-counter has indeed flipped the designated switch at least once; and liveness, meaning that the counter eventually reaches the completion condition and the prisoners are ultimately freed.

desc_declarative_claude:
The module models the classic prisoner puzzle involving a single lamp, where a group of prisoners must collectively determine when all of them have visited a special cell. The `CONSTANTS` are `Prisoner`, the set of participating prisoners, and `Light_Unknown`, a boolean indicating whether the lamp's initial state is uncertain. The `VARIABLES` track the counter's running count, whether a victory announcement has been made, how many times each non-counter prisoner has signalled, the current state of the lamp, and the warden's ground-truth record of who has actually visited.

One prisoner is deterministically designated as the counter, initialized with a count of one to account for themselves. Non-counter prisoners turn the lamp on (at most once normally, or twice in the unknown-initial-state variant) when they enter and find it off. The counter turns the lamp off and increments their count whenever they find it on. Victory is announced when the count reaches `N` (known variant) or `2N − 1` (unknown variant). The warden nondeterministically selects any prisoner to visit the cell each step, updating the ground-truth visitation set. Weak fairness on each prisoner's warden action ensures every prisoner is eventually selected infinitely often. The temporal property `Terminating` asserts that an announcement is eventually made. The invariants `TypeOK` enforces type correctness, and `VictoryOK` ensures that an announcement is never made erroneously — that is, only when all prisoners have genuinely visited the cell.
desc_intent:
Specify a TLA+ model of the classic prisoner lamp puzzle. There are N prisoners, each held in solitary confinement. A warden repeatedly selects any prisoner and places them alone in a special cell containing a single lamp that can be either on or off. After visiting, the prisoner is returned to their cell. Prisoners may communicate and agree on a strategy before the game begins but cannot communicate afterward.

At any point, a prisoner may announce to the warden that all prisoners have visited the cell at least once. If correct, all are freed; if wrong, they remain imprisoned forever.

The system should model two variants controlled by a configuration flag: one where the lamp's initial state is known to be off, and one where it is unknown. In the known-off variant one designated prisoner acts as a counter, turning the lamp off and incrementing a count whenever they find it on, declaring victory at count N. Non-counter prisoners turn the lamp on at most once when they find it off. In the unknown variant, non-counter prisoners may signal twice and the counter's threshold rises to 2N−1.

The warden must be fair, eventually selecting every prisoner so progress is possible. The specification must guarantee two properties: safety, meaning victory is never declared unless every prisoner has truly visited the cell, and liveness, meaning the prisoners eventually win.

This module specifies the Paxos consensus protocol without explicit leaders or learners, modeling the exchange of prepare, promise, accept, accepted, and decide messages among proposers and acceptors. The state tracks all sent messages, a representative decision value, and for each acceptor the highest ballot seen, the highest ballot accepted, and the corresponding accepted value; quorums are assumed to be strict majorities with pairwise intersection. The specification checks type correctness, a non-triviality safety property stating that only proposed values can be learned, and a consistency-related temporal property over the decision variable, while explicitly setting liveness to FALSE and noting in comments that Paxos does not guarantee termination under the asynchronous fault model implied by FLP-style reasoning.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies the classic Paxos consensus protocol without explicit leader or learner roles. It models four replicas acting as both proposers and acceptors over a fixed set of ballots and values, with quorums defined as any three-of-four majority subsets of replicas.

The state consists of a global message set (`messages`) and per-acceptor variables tracking the highest ballot seen (`maxBallot`), the highest ballot at which a value was accepted (`maxVBallot`), the corresponding accepted value (`maxValue`), and a single `decision` variable representing any learnt value. The five actions implement standard Paxos phases: `PaxosPrepare` broadcasts a Phase 1a prepare for any nonzero ballot; `PaxosPromise` has an acceptor respond with a Phase 1b promise when the incoming ballot exceeds its current maximum; `PaxosAccept` fires when a proposer has collected Phase 1b responses from a full quorum and sends a Phase 2a accept carrying either the value associated with the highest previously accepted ballot (via `ForcedValue`) or any freely chosen value if no prior acceptance exists; `PaxosAccepted` has an acceptor record and broadcast a Phase 2b acceptance when the ballot is at least its current maximum; and `PaxosDecide` sets `decision` once a quorum has sent matching Phase 2b messages for a ballot. The temporal specification requires strong fairness on `PaxosDecide`. Safety is checked via `PaxosNontriviality` (only proposed values are learnt) and `PaxosConsistency` (the decision value never changes once set), while liveness is explicitly declared `FALSE`, acknowledging FLP impossibility.
desc_intent:
Specify the classic Paxos consensus protocol without explicit leaders or learners. The system consists of a fixed set of replicas acting as both proposers and acceptors, a set of possible values, a set of ballot numbers (including zero as a sentinel), and a collection of quorums — each quorum being a strict majority subset of replicas such that any two quorums intersect.

The protocol proceeds in two phases. In Phase 1, a proposer broadcasts a Prepare message for some ballot to all acceptors; each acceptor that has not yet seen a higher ballot responds with a Promise carrying its highest previously accepted ballot and value. In Phase 2, a proposer that has collected promises from a full quorum selects a value — constrained to the value paired with the highest accepted ballot among the promises if any acceptor previously accepted one, otherwise freely chosen — and broadcasts an Accept request; acceptors that have not promised a higher ballot record the value and broadcast an Accepted acknowledgment. A decision is recorded when a quorum of acceptors has sent Accepted messages for the same ballot.

The specification must enforce two safety properties: non-triviality, meaning only values that were actually proposed can be decided, and consistency, meaning once a value is decided it never changes. The system need not guarantee liveness, reflecting the FLP impossibility result, so the only liveness obligation is strong fairness on the decide action.

This module specifies a randomized-input variant of a spanning-tree construction algorithm over a graph whose node set is given by Nodes and whose root is Root. The graph edges are not declared as a constant; instead, Edges is defined using TLC's RandomElement to choose, for each node, a random subset of the other nodes, yielding a randomly generated undirected graph for model checking. The state consists of parent pointers mom and distance estimates dist, initialized so every node points to itself and only the root has distance 0; the Next action lets a node adopt a neighbor with a strictly smaller distance and choose an intermediate smaller distance value. The specification checks type correctness, a postcondition characterizing a rooted spanning-tree or unreachable nodes, a safety property stating that quiescence implies the postcondition, a liveness property that eventually the postcondition holds, and a fairness-based progress condition in Spec using WF_vars(Next).
desc_declarative_claude:
The module is a randomized testing variant of a spanning-tree algorithm specification. Rather than accepting a fixed graph topology as a constant, it generates a random undirected graph over a declared set of `Nodes` by using TLC's `RandomElement` operator to pick, for each node, a random subset of its potential neighbors, forming the defined constant `Edges`. The constants `Nodes`, `Root`, and `MaxCardinality` are declared, with assumptions requiring that `Root` belongs to `Nodes` and that `MaxCardinality` is a natural number at least as large as the cardinality of `Nodes`.

The two variables `mom` and `dist` represent, for each node, its current parent in the spanning tree and its current distance estimate from `Root`. Initially, every node is its own parent, the root has distance 0, and all other nodes have distance `MaxCardinality`. Each step of `Next` picks a node `n` and a neighbor `m` such that `m`'s distance is strictly less than `n`'s distance minus one, then non-deterministically reduces `n`'s distance to some value in the range `(dist[m]+1)..(dist[n]-1)` and sets `n`'s parent to `m`. The specification `Spec` combines this initial condition and next-state relation with weak fairness on `Next`. The `PostCondition` asserts that, at termination, every node is either the root at distance 0, unreachable at distance `MaxCardinality` with all neighbors equally unreachable, or at a distance one greater than its parent. The module checks `TypeOK` as an invariant and verifies both `Safety` (post-condition holds whenever no further steps are enabled) and `Liveness` (the post-condition is eventually reached) on a randomly chosen six-node graph.
desc_intent: Write a TLA+ specification for a distributed spanning-tree algorithm running on a randomly generated undirected graph. The graph is constructed over a fixed set of nodes with a designated root, where edges are chosen randomly so that different model-checking runs exercise different topologies. Each node maintains a distance estimate and a parent pointer. Initially the root has distance zero and all other nodes have distance equal to some large upper bound (at least the number of nodes), with every node pointing to itself as its own parent. At each step, some node may improve its distance by adopting a neighbor as its parent, provided that neighbor's current distance is strictly less than the node's current distance minus one, and the new distance falls strictly between the neighbor's distance plus one and the node's current distance. The algorithm terminates when no such improvement is possible. The key correctness properties are: safety, meaning that whenever the algorithm is quiescent the result is a valid spanning tree or correctly identifies unreachable nodes; and liveness, meaning the algorithm eventually reaches that quiescent state. Reachable nodes must end up with a distance equal to their parent's distance plus one, while nodes with no path to the root retain the maximum-cardinality distance with no reachable neighbors.

The module specifies a spanning-tree algorithm for an undirected graph with a designated root node. The graph is represented by constants `Nodes`, `Edges`, `Root`, and `MaxCardinality` (an upper bound on the node count used in place of infinity). An assumption block enforces that `Root` is in `Nodes`, every edge is a two-element subset of `Nodes`, and `MaxCardinality` is a natural number at least as large as the cardinality of `Nodes`.

The two variables are `mom`, a function mapping each node to its designated parent, and `dist`, a function mapping each node to its current distance estimate from the root. Initially, `dist[Root] = 0`, all other nodes have `dist[n] = MaxCardinality`, and `mom[n] = n` for all nodes. The `Next` action non-deterministically picks a node `n` and a neighbor `m` such that `dist[m] + 1 < dist[n]`, then sets `dist[n]` to some value `d` strictly between `dist[m]` and `dist[n]` (inclusive of `dist[m]+1` but exclusive of `dist[n]`), and sets `mom[n] = m`. The temporal specification `Spec` combines `Init`, the always-`Next` safety frame, and weak fairness of `Next`, ensuring the algorithm cannot stall while a step remains enabled.

The postcondition characterizes correct termination: the root has distance 0 and is its own parent; unreachable nodes retain `dist = MaxCardinality` and `mom[n] = n` with all neighbors also at `MaxCardinality`; and all other nodes have their distance equal to `dist[mom[n]] + 1` with `mom[n]` an actual neighbor. The checked properties are `TypeOK` (an invariant), `Safety` (whenever `Next` is disabled the postcondition holds), and `Liveness` (the algorithm eventually terminates). The model instantiates a five-node, seven-edge connected graph with `Root = n1`.
desc_intent:
Specify a spanning-tree algorithm for an undirected graph. Given a fixed set of nodes, a set of undirected edges (each edge represented as a two-element set of distinct nodes), a distinguished root node, and an upper bound on the number of nodes, the algorithm must compute a parent function that encodes a rooted spanning tree. Each node tracks its distance from the root, initialized to zero for the root and to the given upper bound (standing in for infinity) for all other nodes. Repeatedly, any node whose current distance exceeds one more than some neighbor's distance may lower its distance to any value strictly between that neighbor's distance plus one and its own current distance, and record that neighbor as its parent. The algorithm terminates when no such improvement is possible.

The key safety property is that upon termination the parent function correctly reflects a valid spanning tree: the root has distance zero and is its own parent; nodes unreachable from the root retain distance equal to the upper bound, are their own parents, and have no neighbors with smaller distance; and every other node's distance equals its parent's distance plus one, with the parent being an actual neighbor. The liveness property is that the algorithm must eventually terminate.

The module specifies a simple asynchronous handshake interface between a sender and a receiver communicating over a single-value channel. Three variables are used: `val`, the current data value on the channel; `rdy`, a one-bit ready signal toggled by the sender; and `ack`, a one-bit acknowledgment signal toggled by the receiver.

The initial state allows `val` to be any element of `Data`, `rdy` to be either 0 or 1, and `ack` to equal `rdy`, meaning the system starts in a quiescent state with no pending transmission. The `Send` action fires when `rdy` equals `ack` (indicating the previous transfer has been acknowledged), choosing a new data value and toggling `rdy` to signal a new transmission. The `Rcv` action fires when `rdy` differs from `ack` (indicating unacknowledged data is present), toggling `ack` to match `rdy` and leaving `val` and `rdy` unchanged. desc_intent: Specify a simple asynchronous one-directional channel that transmits values from a sender to a receiver using a ready/acknowledge handshake protocol.
